title: Music in One Level
objective: After this level you can describe what turns sound into music: rhythm, melody and harmony.
summary: Every one of 315 societies studied makes music. Music is built from rhythm (when sounds happen), melody (a line of notes) and, in most Western music, harmony (notes at once).

cards.headline: Every society scientists have checked makes music. Every single one.
cards.body: In 2019, a Harvard-led team combed through records of 315 societies around the world. Music turned up in all of them, and lullabies and dance songs were everywhere. So what is this thing every human group makes? This level gives you the recipe.

cards.headline: Ingredient 1: rhythm, the when
cards.body: Britannica defines music as sounds combined for beauty of form or emotional expression, usually by a culture's standards of rhythm, melody and, in most Western music, harmony. Start with rhythm: the pattern of when sounds happen, long and short, over a steady beat. Clap along to a song you love without singing a note. What your hands are keeping is the song's rhythm.

items.label: Rhythm
points: Long and short, over a steady beat

items.label: Harmony
points: Two or more notes at the same time

mascot.line: Keep this: rhythm and melody are the core. Harmony is a layer on top.

cards.headline: Harmony is the optional extra
cards.body: Look again at that definition: rhythm and melody are there for music in general, but harmony only for most Western music. So harmony is a layer, not a requirement. Hum a tune alone in the shower and you're making music with two ingredients: a melody, the line of notes, riding on a rhythm. The next eight levels take the ingredients apart, starting with the raw material: sound itself.

title: What Sound Is
objective: After this level you can explain sound as vibrations traveling through the air.
summary: Sound is a pressure wave: a vibrating object squeezes the air, and the squeezes pass outward at about 343 m/s until they shake your eardrum. With no air, as in space, there is no sound.

cards.headline: In space, a guitar makes no sound at all.
cards.body: Strum one in the vacuum of space and the strings still wobble back and forth. Nobody hears a thing. Sound can't cross empty space: it needs air, water or something solid to travel through. Why that is tells you exactly what sound is.

cards.headline: Sound is a squeeze, passed along
cards.body: A plucked string swings back and forth, shoving the air beside it. Each shove squeezes the air together (a compression), and each swing back leaves it thinner (a rarefaction). Those squeezes travel outward as a pressure wave. The air itself doesn't fly across the room to you. Its molecules jiggle back and forth in place and hand the push along, like a squeeze running down a Slinky.

cards.fact: Sound crosses about 343 meters of air every second.
cards.context: That's at 20°C, and it's quick, but light is enormously quicker. That's why you see lightning before you hear its thunder. Count the seconds between flash and rumble: every 3 seconds means the strike was about a kilometer away.

cards.headline: The last step happens in you
cards.body: When the wave reaches you, it pushes on your eardrum, and your eardrum vibrates along with it, passing the motion to three tiny bones in your middle ear. So every song you've ever heard arrived the same way: as air pressing on a thin membrane, again and again. Music, underneath everything, is organized air pressure.

title: Pitch
objective: After this level you can explain how the speed of a vibration sets how high or low a note sounds.
summary: Pitch is frequency: faster vibrations sound higher. The tuning A is 440 Hz (agreed in 1939, ISO 16). Human hearing runs from about 20 Hz to 20 kHz, and the top end fades with age.

cards.headline: There's an international standard for one musical note.
cards.body: It's the A above middle C, the note instruments tune to, and its official number is 440. Four hundred and forty what, exactly? The answer is the whole secret of high and low notes.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing from this level, make it this: higher means faster.

cards.headline: Pitch is how fast the air shakes
cards.body: Remember Level 2's string, squeezing the air? How many times per second it vibrates is its frequency, counted in hertz (Hz). Your ear hears frequency as pitch: faster vibrations sound higher, slower ones lower. So that standard A is the air being squeezed and released 440 times every second. High and low, in music, really means fast and slow.

cards.fact: Before 1939, an A in France wasn't an A in Britain.
cards.context: France's official pitch put the A at 435 Hz, while Britain's Old Philharmonic Pitch pushed it above 450. A band's instruments had to match whatever pitch its town used. In 1939 an international conference settled on 440 Hz, and in 1975 the standard was confirmed as ISO 16.

cards.headline: Your ears have a range, and it shrinks
cards.body: Human hearing runs from about 20 Hz, a deep rumble, to about 20,000 Hz (20 kHz), a thin whine. The top end doesn't last forever. With age, hearing loss most often takes the high pitches first, like a phone ringing or a microwave beeping, while low pitches often stay clear. A very high tone a teenager hears easily may be silent to their grandparent.

title: Rhythm and Beat
objective: After this level you can explain beat, tempo and rhythm.
summary: The beat is the steady pulse, tempo is its speed in beats per minute, meter groups beats in twos or threes, and rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds laid over the beat.

cards.headline: Tap your foot to a song, and you've found its beat.
cards.body: You didn't count or read anything. You just locked onto a steady pulse. That pulse, how fast it goes and how it groups are three different things, and musicians have a word for each.

cards.headline: Tempo: how fast the pulse goes
cards.body: Tempo is the speed of the beat, usually counted in beats per minute (BPM). At 60 BPM you get one beat every second, like a clock's second hand; at 120 it's twice as fast. Older scores name the speed in Italian instead: adagio means slow, andante is a walking pace, allegro is fast and presto is very fast.

cards.headline: Meter: beats travel in groups
cards.body: Listen longer and the beats start to group. You hear some as strong and some as weak, usually in twos or threes, and each group fills one measure (or bar). In twos, it's ONE-two, ONE-two. In threes, it's ONE-two-three: the count of a waltz, which is danced in 3/4 time, three beats to a measure.

mascot.line: People mix these three up. Tempo is how fast, meter is how beats group, rhythm is the pattern.

cards.headline: Rhythm: the pattern on top
cards.body: Now back to Level 1's first ingredient. Rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds laid over the beat. The beat ticks steadily underneath; the rhythm plays with it, landing on some ticks, skipping others, squeezing quick notes in between. That's why two songs at the same tempo can feel nothing alike: same clock, different rhythm.

title: Melody
objective: After this level you can explain what a melody is and what makes one memorable.
summary: A melody is a line of notes with a contour, rising and falling by steps and leaps. We remember it as relationships between notes, so it survives new words and a new starting note.

cards.headline: You learned the alphabet to a song about a star.
cards.body: "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star", the alphabet song and "Baa, Baa, Black Sheep" all share one melody. It was first published in France in 1761, with no words at all, and nobody knows who wrote it. What is a melody, if it can wear three different sets of words?

cards.headline: A melody is a line with a shape
cards.body: A melody is a sequence of single notes heard as one line: the part you hum. Every melody has a contour, the shape it traces as it rises, falls or arches. It gets there in two kinds of moves: steps, to a neighboring note, and leaps, jumping over several at once. Draw a melody in the air with your finger, and you're drawing its contour.

cards.headline: The same tune, starting anywhere
cards.body: Here's the strange part. Sing Twinkle starting low, then again starting high. Every single note changed, yet it's obviously the same song. That's because you hear a melody as relationships: how far each note is from the last, and which way it moves. Keep those and you can move a tune to any starting note, and most people will still know it instantly.

cards.headline: The words change; the shape doesn't
cards.body: Now the hook makes sense. The alphabet, the star and the sheep all ride the same contour: the same steps and leaps, in the same order. Swap the words or the starting note and the melody survives, because what you remember isn't a list of exact notes. It's the shape. No wonder a melody is so often the most recognizable part of a piece.

title: Harmony and Chords
objective: After this level you can explain how notes combine into chords.
summary: A triad stacks a root, third and fifth, like C-E-G. Consonance sounds stable, dissonance tense, and a 2016 study suggests preferring consonance is learned.

cards.headline: Press C, E and G together, and three notes become one sound.
cards.body: Played one after another, they're a little tune. Played at once, they blend into a single, settled sound: a chord. That's harmony, Level 1's third ingredient, and the three keys follow a simple recipe.

cards.headline: Chords are stacked thirds
cards.body: A three-note chord is called a triad, and traditional Western harmony builds it by stacking. Start on any white key (the root), skip one and press the next (the third), skip one again (the fifth). From C you get C, E, G: the C major triad. From G you get G, B, D. Same recipe, new chord.

cards.headline: Calm chords and tense chords
cards.body: Some combinations sound stable and restful: consonance. Others clash and create tension: dissonance. Traditional theory counts seconds, two neighboring keys like E and F, as dissonant, and thirds and fifths as consonant. Music needs both, like a story needs a problem before its ending: tension builds, then resolves back home.

cards.fact: In one study, a people in the Amazon liked clashing chords as much as calm ones.
cards.context: In 2016, researchers played chords to the Tsimane' of Bolivia, who had heard little Western music. They could tell consonant from dissonant, but rated both equally pleasant. Americans, especially musicians, strongly preferred consonance. The researchers concluded the preference isn't innate: it grows from the music you know.

title: Major and Minor
objective: After this level you can explain why major keys often sound bright and minor keys darker.
summary: A minor triad lowers the major third by one semitone. Hearing minor as sad is largely learned: children use it from about age 6, and it is weak where Western music is unfamiliar.

cards.headline: Move one note by one key, and a chord changes its mood.
cards.body: Play C-E-G, then lower only the middle note to E-flat, the black key right beside it. Many listeners hear the first as bright and the second as darker, even sad. Same root, same fifth, one key moved. So where does the sadness live: in the notes, or in the listener?

mascot.line: Keep this: major and minor differ by one semitone, and it's all in the third.

cards.headline: The whole difference is one semitone
cards.body: A semitone, or half step, is the smallest step on a keyboard: from one key to the very next, black or white. Remember Level 6's triad of root, third and fifth. In a major triad, the third sits four semitones above the root (C up to E). In a minor triad, it sits three (C up to E-flat). The fifth stays put. One tiny step, and the chord changes its name.

cards.headline: Is minor really sad? Ask a five-year-old
cards.body: In a 2001 study, children heard happy and sad music. At 3 and 4 they couldn't reliably tell which was which. Five-year-olds went by tempo alone: fast meant happy. Only from about age 6 did they also use major versus minor, as adults do. Speed is a clue kids use early; the mood of minor is one they pick up later.

cards.fact: In remote Papua New Guinea, major didn't reliably sound happier than minor.
cards.context: A 2022 study played major and minor music to 170 people in communities with differing contact with Western music. The "major is happy" link was strongly tied to how much Western-style music, such as church hymns, people heard. The authors couldn't rule out a small universal effect, but the pattern points mainly to culture.

title: Scales and Octaves
objective: After this level you can explain what a scale is and how octaves work.
summary: An octave doubles the frequency (440 Hz to 880 Hz). A scale picks notes inside it: the major scale follows a set pattern of tones and semitones; other traditions use other ladders.

cards.headline: The 440 Hz A has a twin at 880 Hz.
cards.body: Double the vibrations and something odd happens: the note gets higher, yet it sounds like the same note. Musicians even give it the same letter. This level is about that doubling, and about how music picks the notes in between.

mascot.line: Hold on to this doubling. Strings, brass and organ pipes all come back to it.

cards.headline: Up an octave: double it
cards.body: Pitch is frequency, as Level 3 showed, and an octave up means exactly twice the frequency. From the tuning A at 440 Hz you climb to 880 Hz; go down an octave and you reach 220 Hz. That's why note letters run A to G and then start again at A. The octave travels well, too: it's a constant in the scales of most of the world's musical cultures.

cards.headline: A scale is a ladder inside the octave
cards.body: A scale picks which notes to use between a note and its octave, and its pattern of steps is what defines it. Western keyboards split the octave into 12 equal semitones, and a tone is two of them. The major scale climbs tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone. Start on C and that pattern lands on every white key: C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C.

cards.headline: Other ladders, other music
cards.body: Twelve isn't a law of nature. Five-note pentatonic scales turn up, in different forms, in most of the world's music, from Native American, sub-Saharan African and East Asian traditions to European folk songs. And Arabic and Indian classical music use intervals smaller than a semitone: notes that fall between a piano's keys. You'll meet some of these ladders in Chapter 6.

title: Reading Music
objective: After this level you can explain how notes are written on a staff.
summary: Written music is a graph: five lines and four spaces, higher meaning higher pitch and left to right meaning time. A clef names the lines, and a note's shape gives its length.

cards.headline: A page of music is really a graph.
cards.body: Up means higher and left to right means later. Once you see it that way, those dots on five lines stop looking like a secret code and start looking like a picture of the sound.

cards.headline: The staff: five lines, four spaces
cards.body: Notes sit on the lines and in the spaces between them, and each position is one letter step from the next. The higher the note sits, the higher its pitch. So you can see a melody's contour right on the page: the dots climb when the tune climbs and fall when it falls, just like the shape you drew in the air in Level 5.

cards.headline: The clef says which line is which
cards.body: Five lines alone don't name any notes, so a symbol at the start does. The treble clef is a curly G that marks the second line from the bottom as G, so its lines read E, G, B, D, F (Every Good Boy Does Fine) and its spaces spell F, A, C, E. The bass clef, a stylized F, marks the second line from the top as F. Stack them and you get the grand staff, with middle C on a short line between.

cards.headline: The shape tells you how long
cards.body: Where a note sits gives its pitch; its shape gives its length. A whole note is an open oval. A half note adds a stem and lasts half as long. A quarter note fills in its head and halves it again. So one whole note fills the same time as two halves or four quarters: pitch up and down, time left to right, length in the shape.

title: Checkpoint: How Music Works
objective: After this level you can connect sound, pitch, rhythm, melody and harmony.
summary: One written A travels from the staff to a 440 Hz vibration, crosses the air as pressure waves and shakes the eardrum; inside the cochlea, each pitch has its own place, high near the wide end.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: follow one A from the page into your head.
cards.body: A single written note touches everything in this chapter. It starts as a dot on a staff, becomes a vibration, crosses the room and gets sorted inside your ear. Here's the trip, step by step, including one last stop you haven't met yet.

cards.headline: One A, from page to ear

events.label: Second space of the treble staff: the A above middle C
A string vibrates 440 times a second
Compressions and rarefactions travel about 343 m/s
The eardrum vibrates along with them
Hair cells in one spot respond to that pitch

cards.headline: Your inner ear is laid out like a keyboard
cards.body: Deep in your ear, the snail-shaped cochlea sorts sound by pitch. Hair cells near its wide end respond to high pitches, like a baby crying; those toward the center respond to low ones, like a big dog barking. Each pitch has its own neighborhood, a bit like keys along a piano. And remember Level 3: with age, it's usually the high pitches that fade first.

cards.headline: The whole chapter in one breath
cards.body: Sound is air pressure, shaking. Pitch is how fast it shakes. Rhythm is when the sounds start and stop over a steady beat; melody is single notes strung into one line; harmony is notes sounding at the same time. Everything else in this chapter, from triads to octaves to the staff, is a way of organizing those shakes.

title: Families of Instruments
objective: After this level you can name the main families of instruments and how each makes sound.
summary: Hornbostel and Sachs (1914) sort instruments by what vibrates: idiophones, membranophones, chordophones and aerophones. The orchestra uses four sections: strings, woodwinds, brass and percussion.

cards.headline: Is a piano a string instrument or a drum?
cards.body: You press a key, a hammer hits a string, and a note comes out. So is the piano struck, like a drum, or strung, like a violin? In 1914, two scholars settled arguments like this with one simple rule. By the end of this level, you can use it too.

cards.headline: Ask one question: what vibrates?
cards.body: Remember Level 2: every sound starts with something vibrating and pushing on the air. In 1914, Erich von Hornbostel and Curt Sachs built a way to sort the world's instruments on exactly that. Forget what an instrument is made of or where it comes from. Ask only what vibrates first to make the sound.

cards.headline: Four answers, four classes
cards.body: If the instrument's own body shakes, like a bell or a rattle, it's an idiophone. If a stretched skin shakes, as on a drum, it's a membranophone. Stretched strings make it a chordophone, and shaking air makes it an aerophone: every wind instrument. A bell and a rattle look nothing alike, yet they share a box, because in both the thing itself shakes.

cards.headline: The orchestra draws a simpler map
cards.body: A symphony orchestra sits in four sections: strings, woodwinds, brass and percussion. That map overlaps the scholars' one without matching it. Strings are chordophones. Woodwinds and brass are both aerophones, split by how the air gets going, as Level 13 and Level 14 will show. Percussion gathers idiophones and membranophones, most of them struck, some shaken or scraped.

mascot.line: Keep this question handy: what vibrates? The rest of this chapter keeps asking it.

cards.headline: So, the piano?
cards.body: Back to the hook. A piano's sound comes from wire strings, struck by felt-covered hammers when you press a key. Hitting is how you play it, but a string is what vibrates, so it files next to the violin: a chordophone. The rule works because it ignores how an instrument looks or how you play it, and asks only what shakes.

title: Strings
objective: After this level you can explain how string instruments make sound.
summary: A string sounds higher when shorter, tighter or lighter; halving it raises the note an octave. A bow keeps it vibrating by stick-slip, and the body, not the string, pushes the air.

cards.headline: On its own, a violin string is almost silent.
cards.body: Strings are thin, and they slip through the air without pushing much of it. Yet a violin is anything but quiet. So where does the sound really come from? And how does one string play so many notes? This level answers both.

cards.headline: Three ways to change a string's note
cards.body: A string sounds higher when it's shorter, tighter or lighter, and lower when it's longer, looser or heavier. Players use all three. Tighten a string and it rises. Press a finger down and you shorten the part that vibrates, so the note climbs. And the low strings are the thick ones: the extra weight drags their notes down.

cards.fact: Press a string at its exact middle, and its note jumps an octave.
cards.context: Halve the vibrating length and the string vibrates twice as fast. Remember Level 8: twice the frequency is exactly an octave. Same string, same tension, half the length: the same note, one floor up.

cards.headline: The bow: grab, drag, slip
cards.body: A bow keeps a string going. Its hair is rubbed with sticky rosin, so it grips the string and drags it sideways until the string snaps free and slides back. Then it catches again. This grab and slip repeats once for every vibration, feeding the string energy the whole time, which is why a bowed note can last as long as the bow does.

cards.headline: The body is the loudspeaker
cards.body: Now the hook's puzzle. The bridge, the little wooden piece the strings rest on, passes their vibration into the body, which is big enough to push the air. So the violin's wood does the talking; the strings just tell it what to say. The violin is the smallest, highest member of its family, which also includes the viola, the cello and the double bass.

title: Woodwinds
objective: After this level you can explain how flutes, clarinets and other woodwinds make sound.
summary: In a woodwind the air column vibrates; opening tone holes acts like shortening the pipe. The air is set going by an edge (flute), a single reed (clarinet, saxophone) or a double reed (oboe, bassoon).

cards.headline: The saxophone is made of metal, yet it's a woodwind.
cards.body: Its tube is metal, originally brass. So why do musicians file it with the clarinet and not the trumpet? The answer lies in the very first thing that moves when you play it.

cards.headline: The instrument is the air inside
cards.body: Remember Level 11's aerophones: in a woodwind, what vibrates is the column of air inside the tube, and its length sets the note. So how does one tube play a whole scale? Tone holes. Open them one by one, starting from the far end, and it's rather like making the pipe shorter, so the note climbs. Your fingers cut the tube to length, note by note.

cards.headline: Three ways to get the air going
cards.body: Air in a tube won't start vibrating on its own; something has to set it off. A flute player blows a narrow stream of air against the edge of a hole. A clarinet or saxophone uses a single reed, a flexible strip that opens and closes like a fast valve on the air going in. An oboe or bassoon uses a double reed: two reeds working together.

mascot.line: People sort instruments by material all the time. The family depends on how the sound starts.

cards.headline: So the saxophone is a woodwind
cards.body: Woodwinds were traditionally made of wood, but now they may be metal too. What sets the family is how the sound starts, not what the tube is made of. When Adolphe Sax patented the saxophone in Paris in 1846, he gave its metal tube a single-reed mouthpiece like a clarinet's. Reed first, metal second: woodwind.

title: Brass
objective: After this level you can explain how brass players change notes with their lips and valves.
summary: Brass players buzz their lips into a cup mouthpiece; lip tension picks notes of the harmonic series. Valves (about 1815) add tubing to fill the gaps; the trombone slides.

cards.headline: A bugle has no valves and no holes, yet it plays a tune.
cards.body: Nothing on it moves: it's a bent metal tube with a mouthpiece at one end. Every note it plays comes from the player's lips and a hidden ladder of notes built into the tube itself.

cards.headline: It starts with a buzz
cards.body: Press your lips together and blow until they buzz. That's a brass player's reed. The lips vibrate against a cup-shaped mouthpiece and set the air column in the tube vibrating. Tighten them and they spring back faster, so they buzz at a higher frequency and the note goes up.

mascot.line: Hold on to this ladder. Level 20 uses it to explain why instruments sound different.

cards.headline: The tube's hidden ladder
cards.body: A tube doesn't accept just any note. It favors a set called the harmonic series: frequencies at whole-number multiples of its lowest note, the fundamental. Two times is Level 8's octave; three and four times climb higher still. Without valves, those are the only notes a brass tube can play, and the player picks among them with lips and breath. That's the bugle's whole trick.

cards.headline: Valves: extra plumbing
cards.body: The ladder has gaps. Valves, invented about 1815, fill them: press one and the air takes a detour through extra tubing, so the tube gets longer and a lower ladder takes over. On a trumpet, the first valve lowers the note by a tone, the second by a semitone and the third by three semitones. The trombone skips valves and uses a slide, changing its length smoothly.

title: Percussion
objective: After this level you can explain how drums and other percussion instruments make sound.
summary: Percussion is idiophones and membranophones, mostly struck. Some is pitched (xylophone, timpani), some not (cymbals, snare). A tighter drumhead sounds higher.

cards.headline: Hit it, shake it, scrape it: that's percussion.
cards.body: Most percussion is struck, but some is shaken, scraped, rubbed or even plucked. That makes it the orchestra's most mixed-up family. Can a family of things you hit ever play a tune?

cards.headline: A skin, or the whole thing
cards.body: Use Level 11's rule. In percussion, two answers come up. On a drum, a stretched membrane vibrates: a membranophone. On a bell, a clapper or a rattle, the instrument's own body vibrates: an idiophone. Either way, the hit only starts things; the shaking surface does the work, pushing on the air like any other vibrating object.

cards.headline: Pitched and unpitched
cards.body: Some percussion plays definite notes: a xylophone or timpani can carry a melody. Others, like cymbals and snare drums, have no definite pitch; you can't hum back a cymbal crash. Even the pitched ones typically mark and push the rhythm, locking onto Level 4's steady pulse, the beat.

cards.headline: Tuning a drum
cards.body: A drumhead behaves a lot like Level 12's string: the tighter it's stretched, the higher it sounds. Timpani, the big kettledrums, use this to hit exact notes, and they're the only drums in a Western orchestra tuned to definite pitch. By the 16th century, screws around their copper shells tightened the heads. They're played in sets of two or more, each tuned to a different pitch; today's standard set has four.

title: The Piano
objective: After this level you can explain how a piano's hammers and strings work.
summary: Around 1700 Cristofori swapped the harpsichord's plucking for hammers: the soft-loud pianoforte. The escapement frees the hammer; dampers stop strings; the pedal lifts them.

cards.headline: The piano's real name is a boast: "soft-loud".
cards.body: By about 1700 in Florence, Bartolomeo Cristofori had built a keyboard he called a harpsichord with soft and loud. The name shrank to pianoforte, then to piano. Why was playing soft and loud worth bragging about?

cards.headline: The harpsichord's problem
cards.body: Cristofori looked after the harpsichords at the Medici court in Florence, so he knew their limits. Press a harpsichord key and a small plectrum of quill or leather plucks the string. Pressing harder doesn't help: the player can't make a note louder or softer by touch. Every pluck comes out at much the same volume.

cards.headline: Hammers change everything
cards.body: Cristofori swapped plucking for hammers. Press a key harder and the hammer hits the string harder, so the note sounds louder. His cleverest part was the escapement: it lets the hammer fall away the instant it strikes, so it doesn't sit on the string and choke the sound. Today's hammers are covered in felt, and the strings are wire.

cards.headline: Dampers and the right pedal
cards.body: Let go of a key and a felt damper stops that string. Press the right pedal and every damper lifts at once, so all the strings can ring freely and notes blur together. Remember Level 11's puzzle: however much a piano gets hit, it's the strings that vibrate, so it's a chordophone.

cards.fact: The oldest surviving piano was built by Cristofori himself, in 1720.
cards.context: It's at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. From the outside it looks a lot like a harpsichord. Inside, hammers wait where the plucking used to be.

title: The Guitar
objective: After this level you can explain how a guitar works and how it spread around the world.
summary: Frets shorten the string; the bridge feeds the top plate. The guitar grew from a four-course Spanish instrument to six strings and Torres's design, with relatives like the ukulele.

cards.headline: The ukulele is a Portuguese guitar with a Hawaiian name.
cards.body: In the 1870s, Portuguese immigrants brought a small four-string guitar called the machete to Hawaii. Hawaiians named it ukulele, which means flea. It's one branch of a family tree that probably took root in Spain.

cards.headline: How a guitar makes its notes
cards.body: Level 12 applies here too. The strings barely sound on their own, so the bridge and saddle pass their vibration into the guitar's top plate, which moves the air. To change notes, you press a string against a fret, one of the note markers across the neck. That shortens the part that vibrates, and a shorter string sounds higher.

cards.headline: One recipe, many branches
cards.body: Wherever the guitar went, new relatives grew. Latin America has its own small guitars, like the Mexican jarana and the South American charango. In Hawaii, the Portuguese machete became the ukulele. Sizes, string counts and names change, but the recipe holds: strings shortened against a neck, and a hollow body to make them loud.

title: The Pipe Organ
objective: After this level you can explain how a pipe organ makes sound from air.
summary: Organs blow air into pipes, one per key in each rank; flue pipes use an air jet, reed pipes a reed; stops add ranks. Double a pipe's length, an octave down; lowest about 16 Hz.

cards.headline: The deepest organ pipes go below the floor of human hearing.
cards.body: Large pipe organs can sound notes as low as about 16 Hz. Remember Level 3: human hearing bottoms out at about 20 Hz. So how does one instrument, built from nothing but pipes and air, reach that low?

cards.headline: A keyboard that plays pipes
cards.body: An organ is a wind instrument with a keyboard. Bellows or a blower push pressurized air toward the pipes. A basic organ has one rank, a row with one pipe for each key. Press a key and air flows into that key's pipe. Each pipe sounds only its own note, which is why an organ needs so many of them.

cards.headline: Two kinds of pipe, many stops
cards.body: Remember Level 13's woodwinds? The organ uses their tricks. In a flue pipe, a jet of air vibrates against an edge, as in a flute. In a reed pipe, a metal reed vibrates, much as a reed does in a clarinet. Most organs have several ranks, called stops. Draw a stop and its whole rank joins in, adding a new voice to every key.

cards.fact: Double a pipe's length and its note drops an octave.
cards.context: An 8-foot pipe sounds at normal keyboard pitch; a 16-foot pipe sounds an octave lower, and a 4-foot pipe an octave higher. Pipes run from 32 feet down to less than an inch, giving an organ a possible range of nine octaves. That's Level 8's doubling, built into the pipes.

title: The Human Voice
objective: After this level you can explain voice types from soprano to bass.
summary: Air vibrates the vocal folds; their tension sets pitch and the throat, nose and mouth shape the sound. Soprano, alto, tenor, bass; men sing about an octave below women.

cards.headline: The first instrument you ever played is in your throat.
cards.body: It has an air supply, a vibrating part and resonating spaces, like everything else in this chapter. It's your voice, and the way it's built sorts singers into a handful of types.

cards.headline: Folds that buzz
cards.body: Air from your lungs passes through your larynx and makes two vocal folds vibrate, a bit like Level 14's buzzing brass lips. Change their tension and the pitch changes, much like tuning a guitar string. Then your throat, nose and mouth act as resonating spaces that shape the sound, the way a violin's body shapes its strings.

cards.headline: Four voices make a choir
cards.body: Four-part music stacks four kinds of voice. Soprano is the highest and alto (or contralto) the second-highest. Tenor is the higher male voice and bass the lowest. Put them together, soprano, alto, tenor, bass, and you have the backbone of a choir. Baritone, the most common male voice, sits between tenor and bass.

cards.headline: The octave between them
cards.body: Men's singing ranges are typically about an octave lower than women's. That's Level 8's octave again: about half the frequency. And since notes an octave apart sound like the same note, a man and a woman singing the same tune an octave apart are still, to your ear, singing the same notes.

title: Checkpoint: Instruments
objective: After this level you can compare how strings, woodwinds, brass, percussion and voices make sound.
summary: Each instrument shakes the air its own way, and each note carries harmonics. Which harmonics sound, and how strongly, is its timbre: why the same A never sounds alike.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale: a flute, a violin and a clarinet all play the same A.
cards.body: All three can play the A at 440 Hz. You'd still tell them apart with your eyes shut. This chapter showed what vibrates in each instrument; one last idea explains why the same note sounds different on every one of them.

cards.headline: Five ways to shake the air
cards.body: Strings: a plucked, bowed or struck string, made loud by a body. Woodwinds: air in a tube, set going by an edge or a reed. Brass: air in a tube, set going by buzzing lips. Percussion: a stretched skin, or the instrument's own body. Voice: two vocal folds, shaped by throat, nose and mouth. Different starters, one job: shake the air.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing from this chapter: same note, different blend of harmonics.

cards.headline: Why the same A sounds different
cards.body: An instrument never plays just one frequency. Along with the fundamental, the note you name, it sounds harmonics: Level 14's ladder of whole-number multiples. Which harmonics sound, and how strongly, sets its timbre, or tone color. Flutes and violins produce all the harmonics, while clarinets emphasize the odd ones. Same pitch, same loudness, different blend.

cards.fact: A tuning fork sounds so pure because it has almost no overtones.
cards.context: Take the harmonics away and a note sounds plain and clear, like a tuning fork. Every instrument in this chapter adds its own blend of harmonics on top of the note. That blend is its timbre, as personal as a voice on the phone.

title: The Oldest Instruments
objective: After this level you can describe the ancient bone flutes found in caves.
summary: The oldest accepted instruments are German cave flutes: vulture bone at Hohle Fels (over 35,000 years), bone and ivory at Geissenklösterle (42,000+). Divje Babe's 'flute' may be hyena-chewed.

cards.headline: The oldest instrument anyone is sure of began as a vulture's wing.
cards.body: In a German cave called Hohle Fels, archaeologists pieced together 12 fragments of bird bone. The result had five finger holes and was more than 35,000 years old. It was a flute. So who was playing flutes in the Ice Age, and could anything be older? This level digs in.

cards.headline: A flute carved from a vulture
cards.body: The maker took the radius, a wing bone, of a griffon vulture and carved five finger holes along it. The surviving piece is 21.8 cm long, a little shorter than a school ruler. When the journal Nature published it in 2009, it was the star of a bigger claim: Europe's first modern humans already had a settled musical tradition. Someone chose this bone, shaped it with care and played it, more than 35,000 years ago.

cards.fact: A nearby cave held flutes even older: 42,000 to 43,000 years.
cards.context: At Geissenklösterle Cave, also in southern Germany, flutes were carved from bird bone and from mammoth ivory. In 2012, scientists from Oxford and Tübingen dated them using animal bones from the same layers. Their conclusion: the first modern humans in Europe were already playing instruments about 40,000 years ago. Music, it seems, came with them.

cards.headline: The Neanderthal 'flute' that might be a chew toy
cards.body: In 1995, Divje Babe cave in Slovenia gave up a young cave bear's thigh bone with round holes in a row, more than 40,000 years old. Its finders said Neanderthals made the holes, and Slovenia's National Museum still presents it as a Neanderthal flute. In 2015, though, a paleobiologist found marks of Ice Age hyena teeth at the holes, and most paleoanthropologists accept it as a chewed bone. So the undisputed oldest instruments remain the German flutes.

title: Music in Ancient Greece
objective: After this level you can explain Greek ideas about music, from Pythagoras to the theater.
summary: Greek tradition credits Pythagoras with the ratios 2:1, 3:2 and 4:3 (the hammer story is legend). Plato and Aristotle thought music shapes character; music filled Greek tragedy.

cards.headline: Pluck a string, then pluck half of it. Same note, only higher.
cards.body: At the same tension, the half-length string vibrates twice as fast, and you hear the octave. Greek tradition says Pythagoras found the numbers hiding behind sounds like this. Then Greek thinkers went further and argued that music could shape who you become.

cards.headline: Harmony by the numbers
cards.body: Greek tradition credits Pythagoras, a 6th-century-BCE philosopher, with finding that the sweetest intervals match simple ratios of string length. Halve a string (2:1) and you get the octave. Take two-thirds of it (3:2) for a fifth, three-quarters (4:3) for a fourth. Remember Level 8's A climbing from 440 to 880 Hz? That's the same 2:1, seen from the frequency side: half the length, double the vibrations.

mascot.line: Keep the ratios, drop the blacksmith. The math lives in the strings, not the hammers.

cards.fact: The famous blacksmith story is a legend.
cards.context: Later writers said Pythagoras heard the ratios in hammers ringing on an anvil. It can't have worked: a hammer's pitch isn't simply proportional to its weight. Pythagoras may have known the ratios without discovering them at all; the first workable experiment is credited to Hippasus, a Pythagorean active after his death.

cards.headline: Music could make or break you
cards.body: Our word music comes from the Greek mousike, the art of the Muses. The Greeks took it seriously. Plato and Aristotle held that music acts directly on the soul and on how people behave, so picking music was a question of character, not just taste. If anyone has ever judged you by your playlist, they were following a very old tradition.

cards.headline: Music at the heart of the theater
cards.body: Greek tragedy was partly a concert. Music had a primary role in the plays of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides: a chorus of up to 15 men sang and danced, and an aulos player supplied the music. A papyrus fragment even preserves a few lines of music from Euripides' Orestes, first staged in 408 BCE.

title: Music in Ancient China and India
objective: After this level you can describe early musical traditions in China and India.
summary: China's Zeng bells (about 2,400 years old) sound two notes each and carry music-theory inscriptions; the ba yin sorted instruments by material. India's Samaveda set verses to melody.

cards.headline: In 1978, a tomb in China held the world's largest set of bronze bells.
cards.body: They belonged to Marquis Yi of Zeng, and they're about 2,400 years old. Strike one bell in two places and it sings two different notes. Far to the southwest, India had its own way of turning sacred words into song. Two ancient traditions, one level.

cards.headline: One bell, two notes
cards.body: The Zeng bells, from Suizhou in Hubei province, are the largest and best-preserved set of bronze bells in the world. They follow a 'one bell, two tones' system: each sounds two notes, depending on where it's struck. And they carry 3,755 characters of inscriptions about music theory, the earliest surviving archaeological documents to show mathematical relationships in music. Remember Level 22's ratios? China was doing the math too, in bronze.

cards.headline: Eight sounds, sorted by material
cards.body: Ancient China sorted its orchestras in its own way. The ba yin, or eight sounds, dating from the Western Zhou dynasty, grouped instruments by what they were made of: stone, earth (pottery), bamboo, metal, skin, silk, wood and gourd. The Zeng bells go straight into the metal group. It's a system you could almost run from a well-stocked craft cupboard.

cards.headline: India: the Veda of chants
cards.body: In India, the Samaveda, the 'Knowledge of the Chants', gathered verses mostly from the older Rigveda and arranged them to be sung to fixed melodies during rituals. A specialist priest, the udgatri, sang them, stretching, repeating and pausing on syllables so the words fit the tune. The words came first; the melody reshaped them.

cards.fact: India wrote a handbook for the whole stage.
cards.context: The Natyashastra, attributed to the sage Bharata and dated between the 1st century BCE and the 3rd century CE, is a detailed treatise on Sanskrit theater. It covers dance, music, poetics and aesthetics together. India's ragas and talas get their own level in Chapter 6.

title: Gregorian Chant
objective: After this level you can describe medieval plainchant and where it was sung.
summary: Gregorian chant: one melody in unison, rhythmically free, for the Mass and the canonical hours. Named for Gregory I (590-604), shaped when Charlemagne merged it with Gallican chant.

cards.headline: In 1994, an album of monks singing reached No. 3 on the Billboard 200.
cards.body: It was called Chant, sung by the Benedictine monks of Santo Domingo de Silos in Spain. No drums, no chords, no pop hooks, just voices on one line. What they sang, Gregorian chant, is named after a pope who reigned from 590 to 604. Here's what it is.

cards.headline: One melody, nothing underneath
cards.body: Gregorian chant is monophonic: the whole choir sings a single melody in unison, with no chords beneath it. Its rhythm is free, following the words instead of a strict, regular beat. In Level 1's terms, it's melody on its own. Harmony, notes sounding at the same time, simply isn't part of it. Picture a crowd reading aloud together, in tune.

cards.headline: Sung through the day
cards.body: Chant accompanied the Mass and the canonical hours, also called the divine office: eight prayer services, from Matins to Compline. Early monastic communities set a full series of hours for morning, noon and evening, so in a monastery, singing was part of the daily timetable, not a special performance.

cards.fact: Named for a pope, shaped by a king.
cards.context: Gregorian chant is named after Pope Gregory I (590-604); tradition says it was collected and codified during his papacy. Its lasting form came later. Charlemagne, king of the Franks (768-814), imposed it across his kingdom, where the local Gallican chant was in use, and in the 8th and 9th centuries the two merged.

title: Writing Music Down
objective: After this level you can explain how Guido of Arezzo and others developed musical notation.
summary: Early neumes only jogged singers' memory. Guido of Arezzo's four-line staff with letter clefs fixed pitch, and his ut-re-mi syllables from Ut queant laxis became do-re-mi.

cards.headline: Becoming a church singer once took about ten years of training.
cards.body: An Italian monk, Guido of Arezzo, claimed his new method cut that to one year. His secret wasn't a better voice. It was a better way of writing music down, so singers could read a tune instead of memorizing it.

cards.headline: Neumes: reminders, not instructions
cards.body: Before Guido, chant lived in memory. Early neumes, signs written above the words, only helped singers recall a melody they had already learned by ear. Later scribes heighted them, placing signs higher or lower to hint at the melody's shape. Handy, but you still couldn't sing a chant you'd never heard. It was like a recipe that just says 'the usual'.

mascot.line: Keep this: neumes jog a memory, but a staff gives exact pitch. That's the whole leap.

cards.headline: Guido's lines
cards.body: Guido d'Arezzo (c. 990-1050) used a four-line staff with letters as clefs, so every note had a definite pitch. Now singers no longer had to learn melodies by rote; they could read them. Sound familiar? It's the ancestor of Level 9's staff of five lines and four spaces, with its clefs marking which line is which.

cards.headline: Do-re-mi began as a hymn
cards.body: Guido also gave notes names you could sing. In the hymn Ut queant laxis, each line starts on a higher note than the last, and the first syllables run ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la. Sing the syllables and you learn the steps. Later, ut became do, which is easier to sing, and si (later ti) was added. Every do-re-mi you've ever sung began as a medieval study trick.

title: Troubadours
objective: After this level you can describe the traveling poet-musicians of medieval Europe.
summary: Troubadours, Occitan poet-musicians of the late 11th to late 13th century, were favored at courts. About 2,600 poems survive, fewer than 300 melodies; one trobairitz song keeps its tune.

cards.headline: The first troubadour we know of was a duke.
cards.body: William IX, duke of Aquitaine, born in 1071, wrote songs in Occitan, the language of southern France. His are the earliest troubadour poems to survive. Over the next two centuries, a whole culture of poet-musicians grew up around songs like his. Who were they, and where did most of their tunes go?

cards.headline: The finders of songs
cards.body: Troubadour comes from the Occitan trobar, 'to find' or 'to invent': a troubadour found new songs. From the late 11th to the late 13th century they wrote words and music across southern France, northern Spain and northern Italy. Favored at noble courts, they wrapped the ladies of the court in poems of love. The idea traveled north and east: trouvères in northern France and Minnesingers in Germany wrote their own words and music too.

cards.fact: About 2,600 troubadour poems survive. Fewer than 300 melodies do.
cards.context: The songs, by some 450 troubadours, were copied into songbooks called chansonniers, but most were saved without their tunes. So for the great majority, we can read the poem and only guess how it sounded. Remember Level 25: a melody that isn't written down lasts only as long as someone remembers it.

cards.headline: The women troubadours
cards.body: Women composed too; they're called trobairitz. The Comtessa de Dia, probably named Beatriz, was active around 1175. Her song A chantar is the only trobairitz song that survives with its music. One tune stands in for a whole lost chorus of women's voices.

title: Polyphony
objective: After this level you can explain how singers began weaving several melodies together.
summary: Polyphony is independent melodic lines at once. It began as organum (c. 900); at Notre-Dame, Léonin wrote for two voices and Pérotin for four; Machaut wrote the first complete Mass.

cards.headline: What if a second voice sang the chant too, on different notes?
cards.body: Around 900, a music treatise called Musica enchiriadis described exactly that. Today we'd call it singing in parts. The idea is polyphony, and this level follows it from two voices to four.

mascot.line: Polyphony isn't a tune with chords under it. Every line is a melody of its own.

cards.headline: Many voices, many lines
cards.body: Level 24's chant was monophonic: one melody, sung in unison. Polyphony means two or more melodic lines sounding at once, each heard as independent. It's harmony, notes at the same time, but built from separate tunes weaving together rather than a melody sitting on chords. Think of two conversations you can follow at once.

cards.headline: Organum: chant plus a shadow
cards.body: The earliest written polyphony is organum, described in Musica enchiriadis (c. 900): a voice added to a chant, the two moving note against note. Often the added voice simply doubled the chant a fourth or a fifth below. Remember Level 22's Greek ratios? The fourth (4:3) and the fifth (3:2) were the Greeks' concords too.

cards.headline: Notre-Dame builds upward
cards.body: At Notre-Dame in Paris, Léonin, the first major composer known by name, is credited with the Magnus liber organi (c. 1170), a great book of two-voice organum. When church music was almost all two-part, his successor Pérotin wrote organa for three and four voices, including the four-voice Viderunt and Sederunt. Polyphony grew the way the cathedral did: upward.

cards.fact: The first complete polyphonic Mass by one composer was Machaut's.
cards.context: Guillaume de Machaut (c. 1300-1377), a French poet and composer, wrote the Messe de Notre Dame for four voices, the first polyphonic setting of the Mass Ordinary by a single composer.

title: Renaissance Music
objective: After this level you can describe music in Renaissance courts and churches.
summary: Renaissance music lived in churches and courts: Josquin worked in both, madrigals used word painting, and the story that Palestrina's Mass saved polyphony is a legend.

cards.headline: Martin Luther had a favorite composer.
cards.body: Josquin, Luther said, is the master of the notes: they must do as he wishes, while other composers must do as the notes wish. Who was he, and where did Renaissance music live? Mostly in two places: churches and courts.

cards.headline: A career between church and court
cards.body: Josquin des Prez (c. 1450-1521) moved between both worlds. He worked at Cambrai cathedral, at the Sforza court in Milan, in the papal chapel in Rome (1486-1494) and at the court of Ferrara. He excelled at masses and motets for the church and at chansons, secular songs, for everyone else. Where the job went, the music followed.

cards.headline: Songs that act out their words
cards.body: Courts loved the madrigal, a secular song for several voices, and late-16th-century madrigals were full of word painting: music that acts out the text. In Thomas Weelkes' 1601 madrigal As Vesta Was from Latmos Hill Descending, the notes descend on 'descending', rise on 'ascending', and 'all alone' gets a single voice. It appeared in The Triumphes of Oriana (1603), dedicated to Queen Elizabeth I.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the legend. Remember what's true: Palestrina kept the words clear.

cards.fact: The composer who 'saved church music' probably didn't.
cards.context: After the Council of Trent closed in 1563, reformers pressed for sacred words listeners could understand. A 1607 treatise started the story that Palestrina's Pope Marcellus Mass single-handedly saved church polyphony. Musicologists call it a gross exaggeration. What's true: Palestrina (c. 1525-1594) was known for keeping the words clear, even amid intricate lines.

title: Printing Music
objective: After this level you can explain how printed music spread songs across Europe.
summary: Petrucci's Odhecaton (Venice, 1501) was the first polyphonic music printed from movable type, in several passes; Attaingnant's single-impression type (1528) halved the work.

cards.headline: In 1501, a printer in Venice did something new with music.
cards.body: Gutenberg had printed his Bible around 1455, but music, with its lines, notes and words all stacked together, was far harder to print. Ottaviano Petrucci cracked it. Then a Parisian printer made it fast.

cards.headline: Three trips through the press
cards.body: Petrucci's Harmonice Musices Odhecaton A, printed in Venice in 1501, was the first polyphonic music printed from movable type. His method ran each sheet through the press more than once: one pass for the staff lines, one for the notes, one for the words. Every pass had to line up exactly. Imagine coloring a page three times and staying inside the lines each time.

cards.headline: Josquin goes to print
cards.body: Petrucci produced 61 music publications. Of Josquin's 20 surviving masses, 17 were printed in his lifetime by Petrucci, in 1502, 1505 and 1514. Level 28's master of the notes could now reach choirs he would never meet, in copies that didn't depend on a scribe's patience.

cards.headline: One press, one pass
cards.body: In Paris, Pierre Attaingnant's Chansons nouvelles (1528) used type in which each piece combined a note with its own fragment of staff, so staff and notes printed in a single impression. That halved the time and labor of printing music, and the method was quickly adopted throughout Europe. Faster printing meant more songbooks, reaching more singers.

cards.body: It's carved on a marble tombstone from ancient Tralles, near Aydın in Turkey, and its tune survives because someone wrote the notes above the words. That idea, getting music out of memory and onto something lasting, runs through this whole chapter.

cards.headline: A song on a tombstone
cards.body: The Seikilos epitaph, dated to the 1st or 2nd century CE, is widely considered the oldest complete musical composition; older notated pieces survive only in fragments. Greek letters and signs above its words give the melody. The words say: while you live, shine; have no grief at all; life is short. Found in 1883, it's now in the National Museum of Denmark.

cards.headline: The chapter in one breath
cards.body: Music began in memory: bone flutes, sung verses, chant learned by ear. Writing it down let melodies outlast their singers, and Guido's staff let people read tunes they'd never heard. Troubadours show the cost of not writing: most of their melodies are gone. Then voices multiplied, from one line of chant to Pérotin's four, and printing, from Venice in 1501, took polyphony off the scribe's desk.

title: Baroque Music
objective: After this level you can describe the Baroque style and its instruments.
summary: The Baroque (about 1600 to 1750) was named with an insult about a misshapen pearl. Its music stood on basso continuo: a bass line plus chords a keyboard player improvised from figures.

cards.headline: The Baroque got its name from an insult.
cards.body: In 1734, a satirical review mocked Rameau's new opera Hippolyte et Aricie as "du barocque": full of dissonance, forever changing key and meter. It was not a compliment. Yet that sneer ended up naming a whole era of music. So what were those listeners hearing? A lot of it was happening underneath the tune.

cards.headline: Named after a lumpy pearl
cards.body: Baroque comes from the Portuguese barroco, an irregularly shaped pearl, and its early meanings were irregular and extravagant. Today historians use it, with no sneer, for Western music from about 1600 to about 1750. Britannica sums up the style as grand, dramatic and energetic, with a strong pull between the melody on top and the bass line underneath, and a taste for expressive harmony. The misshapen pearl got the last laugh.

mascot.line: Hold on to the continuo. Level 36 shows why it disappeared.

cards.headline: The floor under everything: basso continuo
cards.body: In the 17th and 18th centuries, music usually stood on a basso continuo, a "continuous bass." A low instrument, such as a cello or bassoon, played the bass line, while a harpsichordist or organist supplied the chords above it. Often only the bass was written out, with small numbers, called figures, hinting at the chords. The keyboard player improvised the rest, a bit like a guitarist strumming from chord symbols.

cards.headline: New forms for a new era
cards.body: The Baroque also gave us forms we still use. Its most important new vocal forms were opera, oratorio and cantata; for instruments, it created the sonata, the concerto and the overture. Several of them get their own level in this chapter, along with the composers who made them famous. Keep an ear on the bass line as you go: it is holding up almost everything.

title: Bach
objective: After this level you can describe Bach's music and why musicians revere it.
summary: Bach (1685 to 1750) was admired in his lifetime mainly as an organist. His fugues and The Well-Tempered Clavier, and Mendelssohn's 1829 St. Matthew Passion, made him the composer musicians revere.

cards.headline: When Bach died, people remembered a great organist.
cards.body: Johann Sebastian Bach ran the church music in Leipzig from 1723 until his death in 1750. In his lifetime he was admired mainly as a brilliant harpsichordist, organist and organ expert. Today he is regarded as one of the greatest composers in history. What did the world miss, and how did it find him again?

cards.headline: A fugue: one theme, many voices
cards.body: Bach's specialty was the fugue. One voice states a main theme, called the subject. Then a second voice enters with the same theme while the first keeps going, then a third, until several lines weave together, each taking its turn with the subject. It works a little like singing a round, but with far more freedom. Britannica calls Bach's fugues unsurpassed in variety and perfection, written for every medium he had.

cards.fact: Bach wrote a prelude and fugue in every major and minor key.
cards.context: The Well-Tempered Clavier comes in two books, the first from 1722, and each holds 24 preludes and fugues. Why 24? Remember Level 8: Western keyboards split the octave into 12 equal semitones. Put a major key and a minor key on each of those 12 notes and you get 24. Bach visited every one, twice.

cards.headline: The comeback: Berlin, 1829
cards.body: The turning point came on March 11, 1829, in Berlin, when 20-year-old Felix Mendelssohn conducted Bach's St. Matthew Passion, its first performance since Bach died. It launched a 19th-century Bach revival that never really ended. The organist Leipzig remembered became the composer musicians revere.

title: Vivaldi and The Four Seasons
objective: After this level you can explain how Vivaldi painted the seasons in music.
summary: Vivaldi, the Red Priest, wrote about 500 concertos in a fast-slow-fast shape. The Four Seasons (1725) paints scenes from sonnets printed with it: program music. It was little known until 1947.

cards.headline: The Four Seasons was nearly unknown until 1947.
cards.body: It sounds as if it has always been famous. Yet before violinist Louis Kaufman recorded it in 1947, it was virtually unknown, and by then the music was more than two centuries old. What had Vivaldi packed into it that made it catch on so fast?

cards.headline: The Red Priest and his concertos
cards.body: Antonio Vivaldi was a Venetian priest nicknamed "the Red Priest" for his reddish hair. From 1703 he taught violin at the Ospedale della Pietà, a home for foundlings known for training its girls in music. He wrote about 500 concertos and fixed the shape we still expect: three movements, fast, slow, fast. Inside a movement, a refrain for the full orchestra keeps returning between the soloist's showpiece passages.

mascot.line: Hold on to the term program music. The Romantics make it their own in Level 43.

cards.headline: A concerto that comes with a poem
cards.body: The Four Seasons is four of those violin concertos, one per season, published in 1725. It is scored for solo violin, strings and basso continuo, and its printed parts included one for organ and cello together. Each concerto came with a sonnet, possibly by Vivaldi himself, with letters marking where each scene happens. That makes it program music: music set to scenes or a story. You are not just told it's spring; you're shown where the birds come in.

title: Handel and Messiah
objective: After this level you can describe Handel's oratorios, especially Messiah.
summary: Handel, born in 1685 like Bach, wrote Italian opera in London until it faded, then turned to English oratorio. Messiah, written in 24 days, premiered in Dublin in 1742.

cards.headline: Handel wrote Messiah in 24 days.
cards.body: In 1741 George Frideric Handel set the whole of Messiah in just 24 days. Today it is a Christmas favorite, yet it premiered at Easter. And the man who wrote it had built his London career on Italian opera. How did an opera composer end up writing Messiah?

cards.headline: An opera composer with a language problem
cards.body: Handel was born in Halle, Germany, in 1685, the same year as Bach, but he made his career in London and became a British subject in 1727. There he composed most of the Italian operas staged by London's Royal Academy of Music from 1720 to 1728. Then the fashion faded, partly because English audiences tired of shows in a language they couldn't understand. Handel needed something they could.

cards.headline: The oratorio: drama without the acting
cards.body: His answer was the English oratorio. An oratorio is a large work on a sacred or semisacred subject for solo singers, chorus and orchestra. Handel's were sung by opera singers, in theaters, with all the drama of his operas, but without stage action. Picture a gripping story told entirely by voices, while nobody acts it out.

cards.headline: Messiah: quick to write, slow to fade
cards.body: Messiah's text was compiled from the Bible by Handel's friend Charles Jennens, and Handel set it in 24 days in 1741. It premiered in Dublin on April 13, 1742, at Easter, raising money for three local charities. And the famous story that King George II stood up for the Hallelujah chorus, so everyone stood? It is a legend nobody has been able to document.

title: The Birth of Opera
objective: After this level you can explain how opera began in Italy around 1600.
summary: Opera grew from Florence's Camerata, which tried to revive Greek music. Peri's La Dafne (1598) was probably the first opera. Recitative carries the plot; the aria carries the feeling.

cards.headline: Opera was invented by people trying to bring back ancient Greece.
cards.body: In Florence, a circle of poets, musicians and thinkers set out to revive the music of ancient Greece. Nobody knew exactly how it had sounded. What came out of their work was something brand new: opera.

cards.headline: The Camerata's idea: one voice, clearly heard
cards.body: The group, called the Camerata, met in Florence around 1573 to 87 under Count Giovanni Bardi; Vincenzo Galilei, father of the astronomer Galileo, was a member. Their efforts helped produce monody: one expressive solo voice over simple chords, a sharp turn from the many interwoven voices of Renaissance polyphony. Out of that grew Jacopo Peri's La Dafne in 1598, probably the first opera.

mascot.line: Recitative talks, aria feels. Keep those two jobs apart and opera makes sense.

cards.headline: Two ways to sing a story
cards.body: Opera sings its story in two modes. Recitative imitates the rhythms and accents of speech, using only a few pitches, and it carries the dialogue and plot. The aria is where emotion pours out in melody. Talk, then feel, then talk again. Handel's oratorios borrowed the same tools: in Messiah, recitatives move the story forward and set up the arias and choruses.

title: The Orchestra Takes Shape
objective: After this level you can explain how the orchestra grew and why it came to need a conductor.
summary: Early orchestras were led from the keyboard or first violin. Mannheim set the four sections; the continuo vanished after about 1770; bigger orchestras brought the baton around 1820.

cards.headline: A composer once died from keeping time.
cards.body: Jean-Baptiste Lully ran a string-heavy orchestra for the French royal court, and he kept it together by beating time with a long stick. In 1687 he struck his own foot with it. The wound became infected, and it killed him. Keeping an orchestra together has always been serious business. So how did we get from Lully's stick to the modern conductor?

cards.headline: Before the conductor: lead from your seat
cards.body: The orchestra's roots run through early opera. Monteverdi's Orfeo in 1607, remember Level 35, used about 40 instruments, and he was the first composer to say exactly which ones to use at dramatic moments. Lully's court orchestra was mostly strings. In Bach's and Handel's day, the composer usually led from the organ or harpsichord, Level 31's continuo seat, or the first violinist led from his desk.

cards.headline: Mannheim builds the modern orchestra
cards.body: In the 1700s, the court orchestra at Mannheim, in Germany, became famous across Europe for its discipline and for effects like long, swelling crescendos. The music historian Charles Burney called it "an army of generals." The Mannheim school set the basic makeup still used today: four sections, strings, woodwinds, brass and percussion.

cards.headline: Why someone finally stood up front
cards.body: Two things changed. After about 1770, as wind instruments won their own independent parts, the continuo was abandoned, and with it the keyboard seat leaders had used. Then in the 19th century orchestras swelled, with three or four of each woodwind and extra brass. Around 1820, Louis Spohr brought the baton from Germany to London, and it caught on. The conductor's core job is pure Level 4: stress the beat so everyone follows the same meter.

title: Haydn and the Symphony
objective: After this level you can explain what a symphony is and why Haydn is called its father.
summary: A Classical symphony has four movements: fast, slow, minuet, fast. It grew from the opera overture. Haydn, isolated at Esterháza, wrote over 100 symphonies and is called the Father of the Symphony.

cards.headline: Haydn asked his boss for a holiday without saying a word.
cards.body: In 1772, the Esterházy prince kept his musicians at his summer palace long after they wanted to go home to their families. Haydn answered with a symphony whose finale falls apart on purpose: player after player stops, blows out his candle and walks off. The prince took the hint and let them go. What is a symphony, that it could carry a message like that?

cards.headline: A symphony: four movements for orchestra
cards.body: A symphony is a long work for orchestra in several movements. The typical Classical symphony has four: a fast opening movement, a slow movement, a minuet, and a fast finale. It grew out of the Italian opera overture, the fast-slow-fast sinfonia played before an opera began. So the symphony is, at its root, an opera's curtain-raiser that left the theater and got bigger.

cards.headline: The minuet: a dance in the middle
cards.body: That third movement came from the ballroom. The minuet was an elegant couple dance in moderate triple time, such as 3/4, and it was typically the third movement of a Classical symphony. Count it and you'll hear Level 4's waltz meter: ONE-two-three, ONE-two-three. The symphony stops to dance before its finale.

cards.headline: Stuck in the countryside, forced to be original
cards.body: Joseph Haydn worked for the Esterházy princes for nearly 30 years, starting in 1761. Their palace at Eszterháza was remote. Haydn later said that, cut off from the world with nobody to confuse him, he was "forced to become original." Far from the fashions of the city, he had to find his own way.

cards.headline: Why he's called the Father of the Symphony
cards.body: Haydn didn't invent the symphony; it grew from that opera overture. But he wrote more than 100 of them, which is why he is known as the Father of the Symphony. He had a sense of humor, too. His Surprise Symphony, No. 94, premiered in London in 1792, is named for one startlingly loud chord that crashes into a soft, gentle slow movement.

title: Mozart
objective: After this level you can describe Mozart's life and music.
summary: Mozart (1756 to 1791) composed at five, toured Europe as a child and wrote more than 600 works before dying at 35. Salieri did not poison him, and the 'Mozart effect' is a myth.

cards.headline: At five, Mozart was already composing.
cards.body: At three he picked out chords on a harpsichord; at four he played short pieces; at five he was writing his own. He would die at just 35 and still leave more than 600 works. A life that short and that full attracts legends. This level sorts the life from the legends.

cards.headline: The traveling prodigy
cards.body: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756. His father, Leopold, was a violinist and composer. From 1763 he took Wolfgang and his gifted sister Nannerl on tours of Europe, with stops in Paris and London. Wolfgang was seven when those tours began, performing for audiences across the continent.

cards.headline: Grown-up Mozart: operas and a Requiem
cards.body: Mozart's more than 600 works include the operas The Marriage of Figaro (1786), Don Giovanni (1787) and The Magic Flute (1791). He died in Vienna on December 5, 1791, at 35, with his Requiem unfinished. His student Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it.

cards.headline: Myth 1: Salieri did not poison Mozart
cards.body: The story that the composer Antonio Salieri poisoned Mozart has no foundation. It spread through Pushkin's drama Mozart and Salieri and, much later, Peter Shaffer's play Amadeus, filmed in 1984. The real Salieri was an important teacher whose students included Beethoven, Schubert and Liszt. Great drama, false history.

mascot.line: Both famous Mozart stories in this level are myths. A good story isn't evidence.

cards.headline: Myth 2: Mozart won't make you smarter
cards.body: In 1993 a study found college students did better on a spatial task after listening to Mozart, and the "Mozart effect" was born. In 2010 a University of Vienna team pooled about 40 studies with over 3,000 people and found no support for a boost specific to Mozart. Listen to Mozart because it's wonderful, not as a brain supplement.

title: The String Quartet
objective: After this level you can explain what a string quartet is and why composers loved writing for it.
summary: A string quartet is two violins, a viola and a cello: one player per part, no conductor. Haydn developed it into a conversation among equals, and Mozart dedicated six quartets to him.

cards.headline: Four players, no conductor, nowhere to hide.
cards.body: A string quartet is just two violins, a viola and a cello, with nobody out front waving a baton. In 1785, after hearing six new quartets by Mozart, Haydn paid him an extraordinary compliment. Why did the great composers love this tiny group so much?

cards.headline: Four equals in conversation
cards.body: Chamber music usually has one player to a part and no conductor, and the string quartet became its star: from about 1750 it was chamber music's main medium, largely thanks to Haydn, known as the Father of the String Quartet. The Classical quartet was an intimate dialogue among equals. Goethe later described it as "four rational people conversing."

cards.headline: Why composers loved it: nowhere to hide
cards.body: With four players, every line is exposed. The Classical quartet was tightly built and challenging to play, and Haydn's Opus 33 quartets and Mozart's six quartets for Haydn became the model later quartets were measured against for a long time. Compare Level 36's swelling orchestra, with a conductor out front. A quartet has one player per part and nobody in front, so the four keep themselves together.

cards.headline: Haydn and Mozart: the quartet friendship
cards.body: In the 1780s Haydn and Mozart played quartets together, Haydn on violin and Mozart on viola. In 1785, after hearing six new quartets by Mozart, Haydn told Mozart's father, Leopold, that Wolfgang was the greatest composer he knew, in person or by reputation. Mozart dedicated all six to Haydn, an unusual gesture, since dedications usually went to wealthy patrons. So much for jealous rivals.

title: Checkpoint: Baroque and Classical
objective: After this level you can compare Baroque and Classical music.
summary: Baroque music (about 1600 to 1750) wove intricate polyphony over a continuo; the Classical style of Haydn and Mozart made one clear melody the norm, with simplicity and clarity.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 finale: when music changed its texture.
cards.body: Bach died in 1750, and the Baroque era is usually said to end about then. What came next, the Classical style that Haydn and Mozart brought to its height in Vienna, didn't just add new forms. It changed how the lines of music fit together. Here are the two eras side by side.

cards.headline: Baroque and Classical, side by side

items.label: Classical, the later 1700s
points: One clear melody leading the way
No continuo; the orchestra's four sections
The string quartet as chamber music's star

mascot.line: Baroque: everyone talks at once, brilliantly. Classical: one speaker, and everyone else nods along.

cards.headline: The big switch: from many lines to one tune
cards.body: The deepest change was texture. Late Baroque music loved intricate polyphony, several lines woven together, like the voices entering a fugue. Classical composers reacted against it: a texture dominated by melody became the norm, one clear tune on top with the other parts supporting it, and forms were built for simplicity and clarity. Level 1's melody moved into the spotlight.

cards.headline: What stayed, what changed hands
cards.body: Some things were handed down and remade. The continuo was abandoned after about 1770, and the orchestra settled into Mannheim's four sections. The Baroque opera overture grew into the Classical symphony. Every level in this chapter is one piece of that handover.

title: Beethoven
objective: After this level you can explain how Beethoven bridged the Classical and Romantic eras.
summary: Beethoven went to Vienna in 1792 and became the bridge to Romanticism: the Eroica torn from Napoleon, the Fifth's minor-to-major journey, the choral Ninth.

cards.headline: He walked into the Classical era and came out the other side.
cards.body: In autumn 1792, a 21-year-old from Bonn left for Vienna to study with Haydn, a master of the Classical style. He never went back. By the time Ludwig van Beethoven died in Vienna in 1827, music had changed direction, and he was the one who turned it. Here's how.

cards.headline: A symphony torn from Napoleon
cards.body: Beethoven planned to dedicate his Third Symphony to Napoleon. Then, in December 1804, Napoleon had himself named emperor. Beethoven tore the title page away, and the symphony became simply Eroica: heroic. At its 1805 premiere it was grander and more dramatic than symphonies were supposed to be. One listener reportedly offered to pay extra if it would only stop.

cards.headline: Four notes, one journey
cards.body: The Fifth Symphony (premiered 1808) opens with three short Gs and a long E-flat: short-short-short-long. Before it's a tune, it's a rhythm you could tap on a table. The symphony starts in C minor and ends with a finale in C major. Remember Level 7: minor to major is one note moving one semitone. Beethoven stretched that single step across a whole symphony, from struggle to triumph.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing about Beethoven: Classical forms, stretched to carry one person's vision.

cards.headline: Then he let singers into the symphony
cards.body: His Ninth Symphony, premiered in Vienna in 1824, ends with a full chorus and solo singers performing Schiller's poem Ode to Joy: the first time a major composer put voices in a symphony. Back to the Eroica: it showed that a symphony could present its creator's view of the world. Classical forms, stretched to carry one person's vision. That's why Britannica calls him the leading figure between the Classical and Romantic eras.

title: Composing Without Hearing
objective: After this level you can explain how Beethoven kept composing after losing his hearing.
summary: Beethoven's deafness was gradual and documented: high notes lost by 1801, the Heiligenstadt Testament of 1802, conversation books from 1818, profoundly deaf by 1824.

cards.headline: One of music's most famous composers was losing the sense he needed most.
cards.body: Beethoven wasn't born deaf, and he didn't go deaf overnight. It crept up on him over years, and he left a trail of letters and notebooks behind. So we can follow it step by step, and see how he kept writing music he could no longer hear.

events.label: Hearing starts to weaken; buzzing and ringing in his ears
Tells his friend Wegeler he can't hear high notes from a distance
Writes the Heiligenstadt Testament to his brothers
Nearly deaf in his right ear; tries ear trumpets
Starts conversation books
Profoundly deaf at the Ninth Symphony's premiere

cards.headline: The letter he never sent
cards.body: In October 1802, aged 31, Beethoven wrote to his brothers from Heiligenstadt, a village near Vienna. People thought him unfriendly, he explained, but he was hiding his deafness: how could a musician admit to failing in the very sense that should be sharpest? He wrote that he had come close to ending his life, and that only his art held him back. He kept the letter private. It was found after his death.

cards.headline: Writing the graph without hearing the sound
cards.body: From 1818, visitors wrote their side of each conversation in a notebook, and Beethoven answered aloud; more than 130 of these conversation books survive. Yet the Ninth Symphony and his late string quartets came after that, composed with his inner hearing. Remember Level 9: a page of music is a graph of sound. Beethoven could no longer hear the sound, but he could still read and write the graph.

cards.fact: At the Ninth's 1824 premiere, a singer turned Beethoven around so he could see the applause.
cards.context: He stood on stage giving the tempos while Michael Umlauf actually led the orchestra. Profoundly deaf, he couldn't hear the hall cheering behind him.
