title: Romantic Music
objective: After this level you can explain how Romantic composers put emotion first.
summary: Romanticism put emotion first. Program music tells a story without words: Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique (1830) turned his beloved into a returning melody.

cards.headline: In 1830, a composer handed his audience the plot before the music began.
cards.body: Hector Berlioz wanted listeners to know exactly what his new symphony was about: a lovesick artist, a ball, a march to the scaffold, a witches' sabbath. That printed page is a clue to what changed in the Romantic era. Music wasn't only meant to be beautiful anymore. It was meant to tell you how someone felt.

cards.headline: Feelings first
cards.body: Romanticism, a movement from the late 18th to the mid-19th century, put the individual, the imagination and the emotions first: feeling over reason, senses over intellect. In music, Britannica says, it meant emotionalism, individualism and nationalism, with richer harmony and new forms built for intense personal expression. Remember the Eroica from Level 41, a symphony as one person's view of the world? The Romantics took that as their starting line.

mascot.line: Program music tells a story from outside the notes. Absolute music is sound for its own sake.

cards.headline: Music with a plot, and no words
cards.body: Program music is instrumental music that carries meaning from outside the notes: a story, a legend, a scene or a personal drama. Its opposite, absolute music, is sound for its own sake. Nobody sings the story; the instruments tell it. That's why Berlioz handed out his program at the 1830 premiere in Paris. Without it, you'd hear a symphony. With it, you'd hear a story.

cards.headline: His beloved became a melody
cards.body: Berlioz had fallen in love from afar with Harriet Smithson, an Irish actress he'd seen play Ophelia. In the Symphonie fantastique, the artist's beloved becomes a melody, the idée fixe or 'fixed idea', that keeps coming back. In the final witches' sabbath it returns grotesquely transformed. The real-life ending was stranger than the symphony: in 1833, Berlioz married Harriet.

title: Chopin and the Piano
objective: After this level you can describe Chopin's piano music.
summary: Chopin settled in Paris and wrote almost only for piano, including Polish mazurkas (accent on beat two). His rubato bends the melody over a steady left hand.

cards.headline: His body is buried in Paris. His heart rests in a church in Warsaw.
cards.body: Frédéric Chopin left Poland in 1830 and never lived there again. When he died in Paris in 1849, aged 39, he was buried at Père-Lachaise, but his heart was taken home to Warsaw's Church of the Holy Cross. How did a pianist come to mean so much to his country?

cards.headline: A composer who lived at the keyboard
cards.body: Born near Warsaw in 1810, Chopin settled in Paris in 1831. Where Beethoven filled symphonies with orchestra and choir (Level 41), Chopin wrote little but piano music: nocturnes, mazurkas, polonaises. His touch was so delicate that it didn't suit big concert halls, so he preferred intimate settings. Think of the difference between a stadium and a living room.

cards.headline: The mazurka: Poland in three
cards.body: The mazurka is a Polish folk dance for couples, with stamping feet and clicking heels. Its music is in triple time, like Level 4's waltz, but with a strong accent on the second beat: one-TWO-three instead of ONE-two-three. Chopin wrote dozens for piano, and Britannica ties his mazurkas and polonaises to his strong nationalist feeling. Far from home, he kept writing Poland's dances.

mascot.line: Remember the name: rubato, robbed time. The tune bends; the beat underneath holds.

cards.headline: Rubato: stolen time
cards.body: Rubato comes from the Italian for 'to rob'. The player stretches some beats and hurries others, for expression. In Chopin's style the left hand keeps a fairly steady tempo while the right hand bends and nudges the melody. Remember Level 4: the beat ticks underneath while the rhythm plays on top. Chopin let the tune lean on the clock without breaking it.

title: Virtuosos
objective: After this level you can explain how Paganini and Liszt became superstars.
summary: Paganini's playing sparked devil rumors; Liszt brought his effects to the piano, gave the first solo recitals (London, 1840) and inspired Lisztomania.

cards.headline: People whispered that his violin playing came from the devil.
cards.body: Niccolò Paganini played so impossibly well that stories spread he was in league with the devil, and even that he'd been in prison for murder. Rumors, not facts. But they show how unreal his playing seemed, and how much attention one performer could command.

cards.headline: Paganini: the violin, pushed to extremes
cards.body: Born in Genoa in 1782, Paganini wrote 24 Caprices for solo violin, packed with the tricks that made his name: glassy harmonics and plucked pizzicato. His tours made him famous across Europe, and his appearances in Paris and London in 1831 were sensations. He wrote them to show off one player, and they still do.

cards.headline: Liszt: the Paganini of the piano
cards.body: The Hungarian-born pianist Franz Liszt heard Paganini play and resolved to carry his violin effects over to the piano. He went further: he gave the first complete solo piano recitals. In London in 1840 he billed his concerts as 'Liszt's Pianoforte Recitals', the first time 'recital' was used for music. Until then, the word meant a dramatic reading.

cards.headline: Lisztomania
cards.body: Audiences lost their heads. Drawings of the time show women swooning and flowers flying at the stage. In 1844 the poet Heinrich Heine gave the craze a name: Lisztomania. His friend Chopin, meanwhile, preferred intimate settings to big halls. Same city, same instrument, opposite ideas of what a concert should be.

title: Verdi and Italian Opera
objective: After this level you can describe Verdi's operas.
summary: After a failed comedy, Nabucco (1842) made Verdi Italy's operatic hero at 28. He paired great drama with memorable melody and wrote Falstaff at 79.

cards.headline: His comedy flopped. His next opera made him Italy's hero at 28.
cards.body: Giuseppe Verdi's comic opera Un giorno di regno failed badly. Then came Nabucco in 1842, and it succeeded as sensationally as the comedy had failed. Suddenly the 28-year-old was the new hero of Italian music. What made his operas hit so hard?

cards.headline: One chorus, a whole country
cards.body: In Nabucco, Hebrew exiles in Babylon sing 'Va, pensiero', longing for their lost homeland. Over time it became an unofficial Italian national anthem. How much it stirred patriots in 1842 itself is debated; the link may have grown more gradually than the legend says. But when Verdi's remains were moved in Milan in 1901, a choir of 820 voices led by Arturo Toscanini sang it for him.

cards.headline: Great stories, singable tunes
cards.body: Verdi took his plots from great drama: Shakespeare, Victor Hugo, Schiller. He paired powerful theater with memorable melody. Remember Level 5: the melody is often the most recognizable part of a piece, and melody was half of Verdi's formula. The hits kept coming: Rigoletto (1851), La traviata (1853), and Aida (1871), which premiered in Cairo.

cards.headline: Still going at 79
cards.body: Verdi didn't fade. At 79 he premiered Falstaff at La Scala in 1893, a comedy after Shakespeare. Remember the flop in the hook? That was his only other comedy, staged at the same theater half a century earlier. Some composers retire. Verdi waited fifty years for a rematch.

title: Wagner
objective: After this level you can explain Wagner's huge music dramas.
summary: Wagner's music dramas run continuously, woven with leitmotifs; his Bayreuth theater hid the orchestra for the 15-hour Ring (1876). He also published antisemitic writing.

cards.headline: Wagner built his own theater, just to stage his own operas.
cards.body: Richard Wagner, born in Leipzig in 1813 (the same year as Verdi), wanted a new kind of work entirely, and a theater built to his own design to match. It opened in the small town of Bayreuth in 1876.

cards.headline: Not a string of songs: a music drama
cards.body: Wagner imagined poetic drama set to one continuous vocal-symphonic texture, rather than separate songs with talk in between. His biggest: The Ring of the Nibelung, four operas totaling about 15 hours of music, first performed complete at Bayreuth in August 1876. There, the orchestra plays in a pit hidden beneath the stage, so nothing distracts from the drama. Bring snacks.

cards.headline: Leitmotifs: a musical name tag
cards.body: To hold 15 hours together, Wagner used leitmotifs, 'leading motives': short musical ideas tied to a character, an object or an idea, which the orchestra develops as the drama unfolds. Hear the motif and you know who or what is in play, even when nobody on stage mentions it. Remember Berlioz's idée fixe from Level 43? Wagner turned one returning melody into a whole web of them.

cards.headline: A difficult legacy
cards.body: Wagner also published antisemitic writing. In the essay 'Judaism in Music' (1850, first under a pseudonym, reissued under his name in 1869), he blamed Jewish musicians for what he saw as empty music. Britannica notes this has been used to explain why he was a favorite composer of Adolf Hitler, and to justify an unofficial ban on his music in Israel. How it shaped his music is still disputed.

title: Music and Nations
objective: After this level you can explain how composers used folk music to express national identity.
summary: Romantic nationalism drew on folk tunes, dances and legends: Smetana's Vltava paints a Czech river; Sibelius's Finlandia hid from Russian censors.

cards.headline: A piece of music once had to travel under a fake name.
cards.body: In 1899, one orchestral piece, with no words at all, made the censors of an empire nervous. It was sometimes billed under harmless titles so it could be played at all. Why would anyone fear a tune? Because in the Romantic era, music had become a way of saying who you were.

cards.headline: Sounding like home
cards.body: Britannica describes musical nationalism as a nation's distinctive features revealed and glorified in music, and it played a big part in the Romantic era. Composers drew on folk tunes, folk dances, folklore and village life. Leaders included Glinka in Russia, Smetana and Dvořák for Czech music, and Grieg in Norway. You've already met one example: Chopin's mazurkas in Level 44.

cards.headline: A river as a national portrait
cards.body: Bedřich Smetana's Vltava (The Moldau) follows the river from its source in the Bohemian Forest, past hunters and a village wedding in polka rhythm, all the way to Prague. It's the second of six parts of Má vlast, 'My Country'. And here's the echo of Level 42: Smetana became totally deaf in late 1874, and he wrote Má vlast between then and 1879.

cards.headline: Finlandia in disguise
cards.body: In 1899 Finland was under tsarist Russia, and its press was censored. Jean Sibelius wrote Finlandia for a celebration that was really a rally for a free press. To slip past Russian censors, early performances sometimes used titles like 'Impromptu' or 'Happy Feelings at the Awakening of Finnish Spring'. Nobody could arrest a spring.

title: Tchaikovsky and Ballet
objective: After this level you can describe Tchaikovsky's ballets.
summary: Swan Lake flopped in 1877 as too dramatic and Wagnerian; the 1895 Petipa-Ivanov revival, after Tchaikovsky's death, made it a classic. The Nutcracker brought the celesta.

cards.headline: His most famous ballet flopped, and he never saw it succeed.
cards.body: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake opened in Moscow in 1877 to harsh reviews. The version danced around the world today was staged in 1895. Tchaikovsky had died two years before. What went wrong the first time, and what went right the second?

cards.headline: Too much music for a ballet?
cards.body: At the Bolshoi in 1877, critics rejected Tchaikovsky's music as too dramatic and emotional, too much like Wagner's dark style, when audiences expected light, airy ballet scores. The choreography was weak too. The complaint is revealing: in a century that put feeling first (Level 43), ballet audiences still expected light music. Tchaikovsky gave them drama.

cards.headline: The comeback he missed
cards.body: Tchaikovsky died in St. Petersburg in 1893. In 1895, at that city's Mariinsky Theatre, the choreographers Marius Petipa and Lev Ivanov restaged Swan Lake. Their version is the one most often followed today. The ballet that flopped in Moscow became the Swan Lake the world knows.

cards.headline: The Nutcracker's secret instrument
cards.body: In Paris, Tchaikovsky found a new instrument, the celesta, 'something between a piano and a glockenspiel'. He asked his publisher to get one and keep it secret, in case the composers Rimsky-Korsakov or Glazunov used it first. It became the voice of the Sugar Plum Fairy in The Nutcracker, premiered in St. Petersburg in 1892. That shimmering sound was, once, a guarded secret.

title: Milestone: Classical Music
objective: After this level you can connect the eras of classical music from Bach to the Romantics.
summary: In 1829 the 20-year-old Mendelssohn revived Bach's St. Matthew Passion. The Romantic century ran from Beethoven's Heiligenstadt Testament to The Nutcracker.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. The century that looked forward also looked back.
cards.body: This chapter ran from Beethoven's Vienna to Tchaikovsky's St. Petersburg: feelings first, stars on stage, nations in sound. But one of the era's biggest moments was a performance of music by a composer who'd been dead for decades.

cards.headline: Bach, brought back by a 20-year-old
cards.body: On 11 March 1829, at the Singakademie in Berlin, Felix Mendelssohn, aged 20, conducted Johann Sebastian Bach's St. Matthew Passion: its first performance since Bach's death in 1750. Britannica says the concert launched the 19th-century Bach revival. So the Romantics didn't only chase the new. They also taught audiences to hear the past again.

title: Music Around the World
objective: After this level you can explain how musical traditions differ in scales, rhythms and instruments.
summary: Musical traditions differ in their scales, their ways of organizing time and their instruments, as the 1977 Voyager record shows. Ethnomusicology studies each music on its own terms.

cards.headline: In 1977, NASA sent 90 minutes of Earth's music into space.
cards.body: Both Voyager spacecraft carry a golden record into interstellar space, its music chosen by a committee chaired by Carl Sagan. Next to Bach and Chuck Berry sit a Javanese court gamelan, percussion from Senegal, a raga sung by Kesarbai Kerkar and a Japanese shakuhachi solo. Play them side by side and they don't sound like one music on different instruments. So what exactly changes from one tradition to the next?

cards.headline: Difference 1: the ladder of notes
cards.body: Remember Level 8? A scale is defined by its pattern of intervals, and a piano splits the octave into 12 equal semitones. Much of the world climbs other ladders. Five-note pentatonic scales turn up, in different forms, from sub-Saharan Africa to East Asia. Arabic and Indian classical music go further, using intervals smaller than a semitone. So a piano can't play every tradition's notes: some fall between its keys.

cards.headline: Differences 2 and 3: the clock and the sound
cards.body: Time is organized differently too. Indian classical music runs on a tala, a cycle of a fixed number of beats that repeats through a whole performance; Britannica notes it has no exact Western equivalent. Much African music layers contrasting rhythms at once (polyrhythm), often over a timeline pattern played on a bell. And the sound sources differ: a gamelan, the orchestra of Java and Bali, is mostly gongs and tuned metal instruments struck with mallets.

mascot.line: Keep this for the whole chapter: hear each tradition by its own rules.

cards.headline: Hear each music on its own terms
cards.body: Level 1's definition said music follows a culture's own standards. A whole field takes that seriously: ethnomusicology, the study of all the world's musics, named around 1950 by the Dutch scholar Jaap Kunst and American colleagues. It depends on fieldwork: studying music where people make and perform it. Folkways Records, founded by Moses Asch in 1948 to document 'people's music' worldwide, has belonged to the Smithsonian since 1987. A raga isn't a major scale with wrong notes. It's a raga with the right ones.

title: Indian Classical Music
objective: After this level you can explain ragas and talas.
summary: A raga is a set of notes with a typical order and characteristic motifs; a tala is a repeating rhythmic cycle, like 16-beat tintal, that resolves on its first beat, the sam.

cards.headline: A raga is more than a scale, and less than a song.
cards.body: Kesarbai Kerkar's track on the Voyager record is one performance of one raga. India's classical music comes in two great traditions, Hindustani in the north and Carnatic in the south. Both build on two ideas this level unpacks: raga for melody and tala for time.

cards.headline: Raga: the notes, plus the rules for using them
cards.body: A raga starts from a set of notes, sometimes different going up than coming down. It also has a typical order for those notes and characteristic motifs the musician keeps returning to. That's what makes it more than a scale. Several hundred ragas are in use today. Northern musicians classify them by mood, season and time of day, though concerts now largely ignore those limits. Performers improvise, but only with the raga's notes.

mascot.line: Don't mix up a tala with a Western bar. It's a cycle that keeps coming home to sam.

cards.headline: Tala: time that comes back around
cards.body: Rhythm runs on a tala, a cycle of a fixed number of beats that repeats through the performance. A favorite in the north is tintal: 16 beats in four groups of four, which musicians track with claps and waves of the hand. The first beat, the sam, is the point of greatest rhythmic resolution. Drummer and soloist love patterns that pull against the cycle, and then they land together back on sam.

cards.headline: How a performance unfolds
cards.body: A Hindustani performance can last well over an hour. Under it all, a tambura, a long-necked lute, plays only the drone: one repeated chord. First comes the alap, a long improvisation with no meter, as the raga reveals itself. Later the tabla joins, two drums played by one musician, and the tala starts to turn. The soloist might be a singer, or a sitar: a long-necked lute with about 30 melodic, drone and sympathetic strings.

title: Gamelan
objective: After this level you can describe Indonesian gamelan orchestras.
summary: Each gamelan is tuned only to itself. A full Javanese set pairs two tunings, five-note slendro and seven-note pelog, and its music moves in cycles closed by the great gong ageng.

cards.headline: A gamelan has no A at 440 Hz. It is tuned only to itself.
cards.body: Remember Level 3's international standard, the A above middle C at 440 Hz? A gamelan from Java or Bali ignores it. Each set is tuned to its own ensemble rather than to any outside pitch standard, so instruments can't be swapped between sets. You can't borrow a gong from the gamelan down the road. What does music sound like when every orchestra has its own tuning?

cards.headline: An orchestra of bronze and beat
cards.body: A gamelan is the orchestra of Java and Bali, mostly gongs and tuned metal instruments struck with mallets. A full Javanese set adds kendhang drums, which guide the flow of the music, plus a bowed rebab, a gambang xylophone, a bamboo suling flute and singers. Gamelan is played for its own sake, and it accompanies dance drama and the wayang shadow puppet play at rites of passage and community festivals.

cards.headline: Two tunings: slendro and pelog
cards.body: A full Javanese gamelan is really two sets, never played at the same time. Slendro has five notes per octave, spaced so evenly they're often called nearly equal. Pelog has seven pitches per octave, with clearly narrow and wide steps, but each piece is built on a set of five of them. So both are five-note systems at heart, the pentatonic idea Level 8 found across the world, climbing very different ladders.

cards.headline: The biggest gong speaks last
cards.body: Gamelan music moves in repeating cycles. One stroke of the great hanging gong, the gong ageng, marks the end of the main unit, called a gongan. Smaller gongs, the kenong, kempul and kethuk, divide that cycle into parts in order of importance. The gongs are the music's map of time: when the deepest sound in the room rings out, one full turn is complete.

title: West African Drumming
objective: After this level you can describe West African drumming and the role of griots.
summary: Yoruba dundun drums 'talk' by changing pitch to follow a tonal language; in Ewe Agbadza a repeating bell time line aligns the drums; griots (jeli) carry history in song, often with the 21-string kora.

cards.headline: In Yoruba music, a drum can recite poetry.
cards.body: Among the Yoruba of Nigeria, dundun drums are used as talking drums, accompanying oriki, praise-name poetry. Talking drums imitate the rhythm and the rise and fall of spoken words. In this level, West African music does three jobs at once: drums that speak, a bell that holds an ensemble together, and musicians who carry history.

cards.headline: How a drum talks
cards.body: The dundun is an hourglass-shaped pressure drum. Cords run between its two heads, and the drummer holds it under one arm. Squeeze the cords and the head tightens, changing the pitch. That matters because Yoruba is a tonal language: the pitch of a syllable can change a word's meaning. So a drum that slides between pitches can follow the melody of speech, and skilled drummers reproduce proverbs and praise songs.

cards.headline: Agbadza: the bell keeps everyone together
cards.body: Among the Ewe of Ghana and Togo, Agbadza is widely seen as the Ewe music and dance. Its drummers play in layers: a low lead sogo drum and a response kidi drum trade phrases over a kagan drum, an axatse rattle, handclaps and the gankogui bell. The bell repeats one phrase, 2+2+1+2+2+2+1, a time line heard across West Africa. That phrase is everyone's reference point, keeping every layer of the polyrhythm lined up.

cards.headline: Griots: musicians who carry history
cards.body: Griots, called jeli or jali in Mande languages, are hereditary West African troubadour-historians. They preserve genealogies, historical narratives and oral traditions, sing praise songs, and have served as advisers and diplomats. Many play the kora, a long-necked harp-lute with 21 strings and a calabash gourd resonator, played with four fingers. In a griot's hands, one song can be a history lesson, a family tree and a tribute at once.

title: Music of the Middle East
objective: After this level you can describe the oud and the maqam system of scales.
summary: The oud, a fretless short-necked lute, is the parent of the European lute. Its music is built on maqam: pitches, motifs and rules of use, with three-quarter tones, explored in the taqsim.

cards.headline: The English word 'lute' comes from Arabic.
cards.body: Arabic al-'ud means 'the wood,' and it's the name of the oud, the lute of the Middle East. Through French and Old Occitan, it became the English 'lute.' The name followed the instrument: Britannica calls the oud the parent of the European lute. Meet the instrument, then the system of melody it plays.

cards.headline: No frets, on purpose
cards.body: The oud has a deep pear-shaped body, a short neck and a fretless fingerboard. Four pairs of strings are the classical number, though five and six pairs are found, and they're plucked with a plectrum. Its present form probably emerged in Andalusia, in Muslim Spain. Those missing frets matter: nothing on the neck forces a finger onto a fixed grid of semitones, so the player can place a note exactly where the music needs it.

cards.headline: Maqam: a mode with a map
cards.body: Music of the Middle East and parts of North Africa is built on maqam: a set of pitches, characteristic motifs and a traditional pattern for using them. Its notes are separated by the half and whole tones Western music uses, plus three-quarter and five-quarter tones. About 50 maqamat survive, but a few, such as rast, saba, hijaz and nahawand, are by far the most used. Level 8's 12 equal semitones are one way to divide the octave; maqam uses finer steps.

cards.headline: Taqsim: a journey that comes home
cards.body: One of Arabic music's most prominent genres is the taqsim, an improvisation. The performer starts in a home maqam, travels through others and eventually returns to where they began. Britannica calls maqam roughly related to the Indian raga from Level 52, and you can see why: a raga, too, is a set of notes plus characteristic motifs. In both traditions, a mode is more than a list of notes.

title: Chinese and Japanese Traditions
objective: After this level you can describe instruments like the erhu, the koto and the shakuhachi.
summary: The erhu is a two-string fiddle with its bow between the strings; the koto, a 13-string zither with movable bridges; the shakuhachi, a bamboo flute Zen monks played as meditation.

cards.headline: A Japanese bamboo flute solo is traveling through interstellar space.
cards.body: On the Voyager golden record is 'Tsuru No Sugomori' ('Crane's Nest'), a shakuhachi piece performed by Goro Yamaguchi. This level meets that flute and two string instruments, one from China and one from Japan. Each has a design trick worth knowing.

cards.headline: The erhu: a fiddle you can't unbow
cards.body: The erhu is a two-stringed Chinese fiddle, the most popular of its kind, held upright on the player's thigh. Its strings, usually tuned a fifth apart, stretch over a wooden resonator covered in snakeskin. There's no fingerboard: fingers press the strings in midair. And the bow's hair passes between the two strings, so the bow is part of the instrument. You can't set it down on top; it lives between the strings.

cards.headline: The koto: slide a bridge, retune the music
cards.body: The koto is a long Japanese board zither with 13 strings over movable bridges, so players can adjust the tuning. They pluck with the thumb and first two fingers of the right hand, wearing picks called tsume. It is related to the Chinese zheng and has long been known as the national instrument of Japan.

cards.headline: The shakuhachi: a flute for meditation
cards.body: The shakuhachi is an end-blown bamboo flute with four finger holes and a thumbhole, derived from the Chinese xiao in the 8th century. Its name is its length: one shaku and eight (hachi) sun. In the Edo period, monks of the Fuke sect of Zen, the komuso or 'monks of emptiness,' played it in public wearing straw-woven basket hats. For them it was a spiritual practice: suizen, 'blowing Zen.'

title: Flamenco
objective: After this level you can describe flamenco's guitar, song and dance.
summary: Flamenco, from Andalusia with an essential Gitano (Roma) role, fuses song (cante), dance (baile) and guitar (toque), held together by the compas, a 12-beat cycle mixing groups of three and two.

cards.headline: Flamenco is three arts at once: song, dance and guitar.
cards.body: In 2010, UNESCO added flamenco to its list of humanity's intangible cultural heritage. Its heartland is Andalusia in southern Spain, and the Gitano (Roma) community has played an essential role in its development. UNESCO describes it as a fusion of song (cante), dance (baile) and musicianship (toque). Take them one at a time, then find the clock that holds them together.

cards.headline: Cante: the heart of it
cards.body: Britannica calls cante, song, the essence of flamenco, and its most profound style is cante jondo, 'deep song.' The singer, a man or a woman, preferably sits, with no backing singers. The lyrics are brief and simple, and they can carry grief, joy, tragedy or fear. In flamenco's golden age, roughly 1780 to 1845, song came first.

cards.headline: Guitar, dance and hands
cards.body: The guitar began as accompaniment, and UNESCO says toque has long outgrown that role. Dance moved to the center in the mid-19th century, after cafes cantantes, commercial venues opening from 1842, put musicians and dancers on show. Dancers use arms, torso, hands and fingers, along with footwork and heelwork. Around them come handclaps, foot-stamping and sometimes castanets, so the rhythm section is often the people themselves.

mascot.line: Clapping along? Count to twelve, not four. The compas is the clock.

cards.headline: Compas: count to twelve
cards.body: What keeps singer, guitarist and dancers together is the compas: a 12-beat cycle with groups of three and two arranged inside it, accented in traditional ways. Soleares, a fundamental form of deep song, moves at a slow twelve-beat pace. Remember Level 4: listeners tend to hear beats in groups of two or three. Flamenco uses both inside a single cycle, and every performer counts the same twelve.

title: Latin American Rhythms
objective: After this level you can describe samba, tango and salsa.
summary: Samba grew from the traditions of enslaved Africans in Bahia; tango from the mixed lower classes of Buenos Aires and Montevideo around 1880; salsa from Afro-Cuban son in New York, built on the clave.

cards.headline: Three dances, three cities, and African roots in every one.
cards.body: Samba took shape in Brazil, tango in Buenos Aires and Montevideo, salsa in New York City. Each is a blend. Samba de roda drew heavily on the traditions of Bahia's enslaved Africans; tango's first communities included descendants of enslaved Africans; salsa is built on Afro-Cuban music. Here's how each came together.

cards.headline: Samba: from a circle in Bahia
cards.body: Samba de roda took shape in the Reconcavo region of Bahia, Brazil, in the 17th century. It drew heavily on the dances and traditions of the region's enslaved Africans, with Portuguese language, poetry and some instruments. Participants gather in a circle, the roda, clapping and singing while dancers take turns in the middle. Migrants carried it to Rio de Janeiro, where it influenced the urban samba that became a symbol of Brazilian national identity in the 20th century.

cards.headline: Tango: born on the Rio de la Plata
cards.body: Tango was developed by the urban lower classes of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, where European immigrants, descendants of enslaved Africans and criollos mixed their customs. Britannica dates it to about 1880, when the Spanish tango, a light-spirited variety of flamenco, merged with the Argentine milonga, possibly with a touch of Cuban habanera. By 1915 it was a craze in fashionable Europe, and by 1920 its music and lyrics had turned intensely melancholy.

mascot.line: Hold on to the clave. Level 60 traces its pattern back to West Africa.

cards.headline: Salsa: 'sauce,' cooked in New York
cards.body: Salsa, Spanish for 'sauce,' is a hybrid built on Afro-Cuban music, above all the Cuban son, which blended Spanish guitar traditions with African rhythms. It developed in New York City, where Puerto Rican musicians such as Tito Puente and Eddie Palmieri played a major part, and Celia Cruz became the reigning diva of Afro-Cuban dance music in the 1960s. It peaked in the 1970s. Under it all clicks the clave: two wooden sticks, and the pattern they play, the foundation of Afro-Cuban music.

title: Folk Music
objective: After this level you can explain how folk songs pass from person to person.
summary: Folk music lives in oral tradition, changing as it passes by ear. 'Barbara Allen', heard by Pepys in 1666, has so many versions the Library of Congress issued an LP of them.

cards.headline: In 1666, Samuel Pepys heard a song people kept singing for centuries.
cards.body: In January 1666, the London diarist Samuel Pepys wrote of the pleasure of hearing the actress Mrs. Knipp sing 'her little Scotch song of Barbary Allen.' Folklore collectors would later find 'Barbara Allen' more often than almost any other ballad. How does a song stay alive that long, and why does it never come out quite the same?

cards.headline: Folk songs travel by ear
cards.body: Britannica describes folk music as traditional, generally rural music passed down through families and other small social groups. It lives in oral tradition: people learn it by hearing rather than reading. And as a song passes along, it varies, reshaped by singers' creativity and by their forgetfulness. That's why a folk song rarely has one 'correct' version. Every singer is a little bit of an editor.

cards.headline: Old songs in the Appalachian hills
cards.body: Between 1916 and 1918, the English collector Cecil Sharp and his assistant Maud Karpeles spent 46 weeks in the Southern Appalachian mountains. He collected songs straight from mountain singers: some of obvious English origin, others, like the square dance, distinctly American. The singers themselves were the archive.

cards.headline: One ballad, a whole album of versions
cards.body: 'Barbara Allen' is one of the ballads folklore fieldworkers have collected most often, under many names and in many versions. In 1966 the Library of Congress released an entire LP of it, Versions and Variants of the Tunes of Barbara Allen, edited by Charles Seeger from its Archive of Folk Song. Same sad story, many different tunes: oral tradition you can hear.

title: Checkpoint: Music Around the World
objective: After this level you can compare musical traditions from India, Indonesia, Africa, the Middle East and the Americas.
summary: Music turns in cycles: Indian tala, the Javanese gongan, the Ewe bell phrase. A West African bell pattern crossed the Atlantic with enslaved Africans; in Cuba it is son clave.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale: around the world, music comes back around.
cards.body: Look back across this chapter and a pattern jumps out. Indian tala, Javanese gamelan and Ewe drumming all build music on a cycle that repeats, and each tradition marks the turn in its own way. One of those cycles even crossed an ocean.

cards.headline: The bell pattern that crossed the Atlantic
cards.body: A Smithsonian Folkways lesson teaches that West African polyrhythmic traditions followed Africans to the Caribbean as a result of the transatlantic slave trade. You can hear the link. Folkways points to 'Gome,' from the album Folk Music of Ghana: its pattern would be called son clave if it were played in Afro-Cuban music. That's the clave from Level 58, the foundation of Afro-Cuban music and the pulse under salsa.

cards.headline: Melody's cousins: raga and maqam
cards.body: Cycles organize time; modes organize melody. Britannica calls the maqam roughly related to the Indian raga. Both start from a set of notes, both come with characteristic motifs, and both invite improvisation inside the rules: a raga performer uses only the raga's notes, and a taqsim wanders from its home maqam and comes back. Across the world, a mode is a way of moving, not just a list of notes.

title: Spirituals and Work Songs
objective: After this level you can describe the songs of enslaved African Americans and their legacy.
summary: Enslaved African Americans created spirituals, passed on only by live singing and built on call-and-response. Work songs kept crews in rhythm; out of both came the blues.

cards.headline: The songs that carried a people through slavery were never written down.
cards.body: Enslaved African Americans made their songs without paper, passing them on by voice alone. Yet those songs lasted, and out of them, in time, came the blues. How did music with no sheet music survive, and what was it really saying?

mascot.line: Keep this shape: a leader's line, a group's answer. You'll hear it all chapter.

cards.headline: Spirituals: passed voice to voice, leader to chorus
cards.body: The Library of Congress describes spirituals as religious folk songs created and sung by enslaved people of African descent in the American South. Through the whole era of slavery, they passed from one generation to the next only by live singing. Their shape helped: a leader sings a line and the chorus answers with a refrain, often over clapping and patting. That's call-and-response, and a song built that way is easy to join and hard to forget.

cards.headline: A Bible story with a second meaning
cards.body: "Go Down, Moses" retells the Exodus: Moses tells Pharaoh to free the Israelites from slavery in Egypt, and the congregation answers, "Let my people go!" On the surface, it's scripture. But it was sung by enslaved people, about enslaved people demanding freedom from a far more powerful master. Music scholars hear in it a direct expression of their longing for freedom.

cards.headline: Work songs: music that keeps a crew in step
cards.body: Work songs had a different job. Singing passed the time and kept a crew moving together, and many crews had a leader who sang a line while the others answered with a refrain. Sound familiar? Britannica traces a long thread from here: during and after slavery, Black American workers built spirituals and, ultimately, the blues out of older work song traditions. Keep hold of that thread; the next level pulls it.

cards.fact: In 1873, a student choir sang spirituals for Queen Victoria, and its tour paid for a college building.
cards.context: Fisk University, founded in 1865 to educate formerly enslaved people, was deep in debt by 1871, so a professor formed a student choir to raise money. The Fisk Jubilee Singers carried spirituals, rarely heard outside Black churches and homes, to audiences in the US and Europe. Tour proceeds built Fisk's Jubilee Hall.

title: The Blues
objective: After this level you can explain the blues form and where it came from.
summary: African Americans created the blues in the Deep South after the Civil War. Its 12-bar form uses three chords and AAB verses; blue notes fall between major and minor.

cards.headline: A bandleader waiting for a train heard a sound he'd build a career on.
cards.body: Around 1903, at the train station in Tutwiler, Mississippi, W.C. Handy heard a man singing while pressing a knife against his guitar strings. It was the blues. Handy, later known as the "Father of the Blues," went on to publish "The Memphis Blues" in 1912 and "St. Louis Blues" in 1914. So what exactly had he heard?

cards.headline: Born in the Deep South, out of the songs of slavery
cards.body: African Americans created the blues in the Deep South after the Civil War, and it was a recognizable genre by the 1890s. Its makers were formerly enslaved people and their children, many still working Southern plantations. Its raw material was Level 61's music: the three-line blues grew out of work songs, field calls, spirituals and folk ballads. The blues is what those songs became in the mouths of free people.

cards.headline: Say it, say it again, then answer it
cards.body: Most blues follow a 12-bar form built on just three chords: the tonic, the subdominant and the dominant. The words come in three-line stanzas. The second line more or less repeats the first, and the third finishes the thought with a new line that rhymes. It's call-and-response folded into one verse: you state your trouble, state it again, then deliver the punchline.

mascot.line: A blue note isn't a wrong note. It lives between the keys, where a piano can't go.

cards.headline: Blue notes live in the cracks between the keys
cards.body: Remember Level 7? A major third sits four semitones above the root, a minor third three, and a semitone is the smallest step on a keyboard. A blue note lowers the third, the seventh or sometimes the fifth by less than a semitone, so a blue third lands between major and minor, where a piano has no key. That's why the Tutwiler man's knife made sense: guitarists bend strings or slide a bar along them to reach the cracks.

title: Ragtime
objective: After this level you can describe ragtime and Scott Joplin.
summary: Ragtime set a syncopated right hand over a steady left-hand beat. Scott Joplin, the King of Ragtime, wrote "Maple Leaf Rag" (1899) and won a posthumous Pulitzer.

cards.headline: Ragtime piano sounds like two hands arguing about where the beat is.
cards.body: Put on a rag and your foot finds the beat at once. Then the melody jumps in just off it, again and again. That friendly tug-of-war made ragtime the leading style of American popular music from about 1899 to 1917. Here's how it works, and who did it best.

cards.headline: The left hand keeps time; the right hand plays with it
cards.body: Remember Level 4's beat, the steady pulse you tap your foot to? In ragtime piano, the left hand guards it with regularly accented bass notes and chords. Over the top, the right hand plays a bouncing melody that keeps accenting notes off the beat. That's syncopation, and to "rag" a tune simply meant to syncopate its melody. The style drew on African American banjo playing and the syncopated dance rhythms of the cakewalk.

cards.headline: Scott Joplin, the King of Ragtime
cards.body: Scott Joplin, an African American composer born in Texas in 1867 or 1868, became known as the King of Ragtime. His "Maple Leaf Rag," published in 1899, was the most successful of the early rags and became the style's signature piece. Joplin aimed high: he wrote a three-act opera, Treemonisha, and published it at his own expense in 1911.

cards.fact: Scott Joplin won a Pulitzer Prize in 1976, decades after he died.
cards.context: Joplin died in 1917. In the 1970s his music came roaring back in the Oscar-winning score of the film The Sting, and in 1976 the Pulitzer board gave him a special award for his contributions to American music. Ragtime itself was one forerunner of jazz, which is where this chapter heads next.

title: New Orleans and Early Jazz
objective: After this level you can explain how jazz began in New Orleans.
summary: African Americans developed jazz in New Orleans from brass bands, blues and spirituals. Segregation pushed Black and Creole musicians together; front-line horns improvised at once.

cards.headline: The first king of jazz never made a record.
cards.body: Between 1895 and 1900, New Orleans cornetist Buddy Bolden began adding improvised blues to dance tunes, and his band is generally considered the first to play what became jazz. His horn was said to carry for miles. No recording of him was ever made, so no one can hear him now. What we can trace is where his music came from.

cards.headline: A city where African music never went quiet
cards.body: By the mid-1700s, enslaved people in New Orleans gathered on Sundays at a market later called Congo Square, famous for African dance and music. The city also loved brass bands, and it heard West African, Caribbean and Spanish traditions side by side, plus the blues and spirituals. Jazz, developed by African Americans, grew from that mix: its rhythms rooted mainly in West Africa, instruments like the trumpet and trombone from Europe.

cards.headline: Segregation pushed two musical worlds together
cards.body: New Orleans had long given Creoles of color, people of mixed African and European descent, a special status. Segregation laws passed in the 1890s wiped that status away and increased discrimination against anyone with African ancestry. One result was musical: Creole and Black musicians were pushed into the same world and, in time, the same bands.

cards.headline: Three horns, all talking at once
cards.body: A classic New Orleans band had a front line of cornet, clarinet and trombone over guitar, bass and drums. The horns improvised together, each weaving its own line around the tune, for a busy, many-voiced sound. Then came a twist: in 1917 the first commercial jazz record was made by the Original Dixieland Jazz Band, five white musicians, playing a style African Americans had created.

title: Louis Armstrong
objective: After this level you can explain how Armstrong made the solo central to jazz.
summary: Louis Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven records (1925-28) broke from collective improvising and made him the first great jazz soloist. He also helped invent scat.

cards.headline: Before Louis Armstrong, a jazz band was a crowd. After him, it had a star.
cards.body: Level 64's New Orleans bands improvised all at once, horns weaving around one another. Then a young trumpeter from those same streets stepped out in front, and jazz never quite went back. How did one player make the solo the heart of the music?

cards.headline: From the Waifs Home to King Oliver's band
cards.body: Louis Armstrong was born in New Orleans in 1901. In 1913 he was sent to the Colored Waifs Home as a juvenile delinquent, and there he learned to play cornet in the home's band. In 1922 King Oliver, then leading a band in Chicago, sent for him to play second cornet. Second cornet is a supporting part. It didn't hold him for long.

cards.headline: The ensemble couldn't contain him
cards.body: On his Hot Five and Hot Seven records of 1925 to 1928, Armstrong left Oliver's collective improvising behind. The short breaks where one player stepped forward grew into full solos, with the band in support. Britannica calls him the first great jazz soloist, and by "West End Blues" in 1928 the virtuoso soloist ruled jazz. Virtually every jazz horn player after him learned from his playing.

cards.headline: He soloed with his voice, too
cards.body: Armstrong sang on many of his records and helped invent scat singing: wordless syllables sung in place of lyrics, used the way a horn uses notes. One of the earliest scat recordings is his "Heebie Jeebies." Voice or trumpet, the idea was the same: one player, out front, telling the story.

title: Swing and Big Bands
objective: After this level you can describe the swing era.
summary: Swing-era big bands played brass, woodwind and rhythm sections off each other. Fletcher Henderson's charts shaped Benny Goodman's sound; Goodman's integrated groups crossed the color line.

cards.headline: The "King of Swing" got his band's sound from a Black bandleader's pen.
cards.body: Clarinetist Benny Goodman was billed as the King of Swing. Yet his band's most characteristic sound came from arrangements by Fletcher Henderson, a Black pianist and bandleader. In a segregated country, that partnership says a lot about the swing era: who made the music, and who got top billing.

cards.headline: A big band is three bands in conversation
cards.body: The swing era ran from about 1935 to the mid-1940s, when big dance bands were at their most popular. Arrangers grouped players into sections of brass, woodwinds and rhythm, then played the sections off against each other: one tosses a phrase, another answers. Hear the echo of Level 61's call-and-response? It's the same shape, now scored for a whole band.

cards.headline: What makes it swing?
cards.body: Swing isn't just a speed. Britannica describes it as a compelling momentum that comes from how players attack and accent notes against the fixed beat. The beat stays steady, just like Level 4's pulse; the notes lean on it and push against it. That forward pull is made for moving, and swing went hand in hand with African American social dances like the lindy hop.

cards.headline: Henderson's charts, and a color line crossed
cards.body: Fletcher Henderson's bands of the 1920s were especially important in spreading the ideas swing was built on, and his charts gave Goodman's band its most characteristic sound. Goodman also hired pianist Teddy Wilson, though he feared the consequences, and Lionel Hampton in 1936. In a time of segregation, those integrated groups gave Black musicians greater visibility.

title: Duke Ellington
objective: After this level you can describe Ellington's compositions and his band.
summary: Duke Ellington wrote for his players' own sounds. His band played Harlem's whites-only Cotton Club from 1927, and he won a posthumous Pulitzer citation in 1999.

cards.headline: Duke Ellington's "Mood Indigo" score doesn't say "clarinet." It says "Barney."
cards.body: In the Smithsonian's Duke Ellington Collection, his short score for "Mood Indigo" (1930) labels lines by player: "Barney" for clarinetist Barney Bigard, "Tricky" for trombonist Joe "Tricky Sam" Nanton. Most scores name instruments. Ellington named people.

cards.headline: Writing for the player, not the instrument
cards.body: Ellington (1899 to 1974), born in Washington, D.C., led his band for more than half a century and composed thousands of scores. He wrote works to highlight the special talents of his soloists, so a part fit one person's sound the way a tailored suit fits one body. "Mood Indigo" blended a muted trumpet, an unmuted trombone and a low-register clarinet into one sound.

cards.headline: The Cotton Club: Black stars, white-only audience
cards.body: In 1927 Ellington's orchestra became the house band at the Cotton Club, a famous nightspot in Harlem, New York. The club featured Black entertainers but limited its audience to white patrons. Black musicians made the music on that stage, and Black listeners were shut out of the room.

cards.fact: In 1999, long after his death in 1974, Ellington got a special Pulitzer citation.
cards.context: The Pulitzer board honored his musical genius, which, it said, evoked the principles of democracy through the medium of jazz. If that sounds familiar, it should: Level 63's Scott Joplin also got his Pulitzer long after he died.

title: Bebop
objective: After this level you can explain how bebop made jazz faster and more complex.
summary: Bebop took shape in early-1940s Harlem jam sessions: small groups, rapid tempos, solos built on chords. Parker built melodies from higher intervals; jazz became music for listening.

cards.headline: In 1939, a young saxophonist was bored with the chords everyone played.
cards.body: Charlie Parker later recalled being tired of the stereotyped chord changes of the day. "I kept thinking there's bound to be something else," he said. "I could hear it sometimes but I couldn't play it." Jamming on the tune "Cherokee" in December 1939, he found it. A few years later, it had a name: bebop.

cards.headline: Born in Harlem jam sessions, made for listening
cards.body: Bebop took shape in the early 1940s in jam sessions at Minton's Playhouse in Harlem, with Parker, trumpeter Dizzy Gillespie, pianist Thelonious Monk and drummer Kenny Clarke. It grew out of the swing bands and pushed against their limits: small combos, extremely rapid tempos, and solos built on the chords rather than the tune. As ballroom dancing declined during World War II, jazz became music you sat down to hear.

cards.headline: Climbing higher up the chord
cards.body: Remember Level 6's triad: root, third and fifth, stacked in thirds. Most players of the day built their lines on the root, 3rd, 5th and 7th. Parker reached higher, to the 9th, 11th and 13th, and made melodies from those upper notes. Bebop players also slipped extra "substituted" chords into older jazz harmonies. The result is rich, restless and very, very fast.

cards.fact: At first, bebop was unacceptable to the general public, and to many musicians too.
cards.context: Swing had been America's dance music. Bebop asked listeners to sit still and keep up, and Britannica notes the splits it opened were deep. The next level looks at the skill at the center of it all: improvising.

title: Improvisation
objective: After this level you can explain how jazz musicians improvise.
summary: Jazz soloists invent melodies on the spot over a shared chord progression; Parker's "Ko Ko" kept the chords of "Cherokee" and dropped its tune. Players also answer in call-and-response.

cards.headline: Jazz soloists make it up on the spot. So why don't they crash?
cards.body: Improvising is one of jazz's defining traits: in most performances, players take solos they invent in the moment. A whole band making things up sounds like a recipe for chaos. Yet a good band sounds like one mind. The secret: they aren't making up everything. They share a map.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing about improvising: the chords are the map, the solo is the route.

cards.headline: The map is the chord progression
cards.body: A jazz tune gives everyone the same road: its melody and, underneath, a repeating pattern of chords, Level 6's chords set in order. While piano, guitar and bass play that progression, with drums, the soloist invents new melodies that fit it. Level 62's 12-bar blues is one such map, used in jazz as well as blues. The chords are fixed; the route is yours. That's how jazz turns a tune everyone knows into something personal.

cards.headline: The tune that tested everyone
cards.body: Some maps are hard. Ray Noble's "Cherokee" runs 64 measures, and from 1938 to 1945 its chord changes challenged many jazz improvisers. Level 68's Charlie Parker mastered them. In 1945 he recorded "Ko Ko," built on the chord structure of "Cherokee" with the original tune left out, so all you hear is the road and his route through it. The Library of Congress added it to the National Recording Registry in 2002.

cards.headline: Improvising is a conversation
cards.body: Jazz players don't only solo; they answer each other. The Smithsonian notes you can often hear call-and-response in jazz, with one instrument, voice or part of the band answering another. That's the shape of Level 61's spirituals and work songs, where a leader sang and a group replied. The oldest idea in this chapter is still how jazz talks.

objective: After this level you can trace the path from spirituals and blues to bebop.
summary: About six million Black Americans left the South in the Great Migration, fleeing Jim Crow. The blues and jazz went with them, from the Deep South to Chicago and Harlem.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 finale: the music caught a train north.
cards.body: This chapter began in the South, with songs created by enslaved people. It ends in Harlem, with bebop. In between, the music traveled a long way. How did it get there? The same way millions of people did.

cards.headline: The Great Migration
cards.body: From the 1910s to 1970, about six million Black Americans left the rural South for cities in the North and West, like Chicago, Detroit and New York. They were leaving Jim Crow laws and sharecropping for more jobs, though racism was rampant in the North too. And they brought their music. Britannica notes that migrants changed the sound of the blues they carried north.

mascot.line: Ten levels, one lesson: follow the people, and you'll find the music.

cards.headline: Jazz followed the jobs to Chicago
cards.body: During World War I, a boom in Chicago meant work for musicians, and New Orleans players went north, cornetist Joe "King" Oliver among them. In 1922 Oliver sent for Level 65's Louis Armstrong, and Armstrong made the recordings that revolutionized jazz in Chicago, between 1925 and 1928. Music moves with the people who make it.

title: Recorded Sound
objective: After this level you can explain how Edison's phonograph first recorded sound.
summary: Scott's 1860 phonautograph drew sound but couldn't replay it; Edison's 1877 tinfoil phonograph pressed vibrations into foil and traced them back out, recording and playing back sound.

cards.headline: The oldest recording of a human voice waited 148 years to be heard.
cards.body: In 1860, a Parisian inventor named Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville recorded a singer performing the folk song "Au Clair de la Lune." His phonautograph scratched the sound's wiggles onto soot-covered paper. There was just one catch: it was never meant to play anything back. So what does it take to put sound in a box and get it out again?

cards.headline: 1877: a machine that could talk back
cards.body: Scott had half the trick. Thomas Edison's phonograph, built in 1877, was the first machine to both record sound and play it back. For his first test, Edison recited "Mary Had a Little Lamb." The recording half went like this: your voice shook a thin diaphragm, the diaphragm drove a needlelike stylus, and the stylus pressed tiny pits into tinfoil wrapped around a cylinder that you turned with a hand crank.

mascot.line: Keep this: recording turns vibration into a shape, and playback turns the shape back.

cards.headline: Playback is recording run in reverse
cards.body: Remember Level 2: sound is a pressure wave, squeezes and thinnings of the air. The pits in the foil were a frozen copy of that pattern. To play it back, a lighter stylus traced the same pits and shook a second diaphragm, which pushed the air into the same squeezes all over again. Vibration became dents, and dents became vibration. The only motor was your hand on the crank.

cards.fact: Scott's 1860 song was finally heard in 2008, from scans of his paper.
cards.context: Physicist Carl Haber of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory pulled the sound off the soot, 148 years after it was made. It became the earliest recording of a human voice ever played back. So the honors split neatly: Scott recorded first, and Edison was first to press play.

title: Radio Hits
objective: After this level you can explain how radio created national hits.
summary: KDKA's 1920 broadcast began US commercial radio; by 1930, 40.3% of homes had a set and networks like NBC reached many cities at once. Payola showed airplay's value and led to a 1960 law.

cards.headline: In 1920, election night arrived through the air.
cards.body: On November 2, 1920, KDKA in Pittsburgh, recognized as America's first commercial radio station, went on the air with the Harding-Cox presidential election returns. What happens to music when a whole country can hear the same thing at the same moment?

cards.fact: In 1930, 40.3% of US households owned a radio: 12,048,762 homes.
cards.context: That count comes from the 1930 census, taken just ten years after KDKA's first broadcast. Put another way, roughly two homes in every five could now switch on a band without anyone leaving the living room.

cards.headline: One studio, twenty-one cities
cards.body: A single station only reaches so far. The fix was a network. NBC, the first organized national network, made its first broadcast on November 15, 1926, from New York over 25 stations in 21 cities, reaching as far west as Kansas City. Now one performance could land in living rooms across the country on the same night. That's the recipe for a national hit: everybody hearing the same song at once.

cards.headline: Airplay was worth a bribe
cards.body: If radio could make a song famous, getting on the air was worth money. Payola is an undercover payment to a disc jockey for promoting a record. In the payola scandal of the late 1950s, deejays took bribes to push certain records, and many lost their jobs. In 1960, largely because of those scandals, Congress amended the Communications Act, rewriting the rules on when broadcasts must say who paid for them.

title: Rock and Roll
objective: After this level you can explain how rock and roll grew from blues, country and gospel.
summary: Rock and roll arose in the mid-1950s from rhythm and blues and country, with gospel fire, led by Black stars like Chuck Berry. Its first record is debated: Tharpe's 1944 song, or Rocket 88 (1951)?

cards.headline: Ask who made the first rock and roll record, and start an argument.
cards.body: Many people point to "Rocket 88," recorded in March 1951 at Sam Phillips' studio in Memphis by Ike Turner's Kings of Rhythm, with Jackie Brenston singing. But the Library of Congress notes that rock and roll grew gradually, and there are earlier contenders. That's the real story: rock and roll didn't have one inventor. It had roots.

cards.headline: Root 1: rhythm and blues
cards.body: Britannica describes rock and roll, which took off in the US in the mid-1950s, as a merger of country music and rhythm and blues. Its first big stars included Fats Domino, Little Richard, Chuck Berry and Bo Diddley, Black artists who only years earlier would have been called rhythm-and-blues acts. Radio helped, as Level 72 would predict: Cleveland disc jockey Alan Freed played hard-driving rhythm-and-blues records that introduced white teenagers to the sound.

cards.headline: Root 2: gospel, on an electric guitar
cards.body: Sister Rosetta Tharpe sang gospel songs while playing electric guitar. She influenced Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Jerry Lee Lewis and Elvis Presley, and some musicologists call a 1944 recording of hers the first rock-and-roll song. In 2018 she entered the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as an early influence. Church music, played loud, was part of rock's engine from the start.

mascot.line: Don't memorize one "first" record. Remember the roots: R&B, gospel and country.

cards.headline: Root 3: country, crossing both ways
cards.body: The roots crossed in both directions. Chuck Berry's 1955 hit "Maybellene" was a country-influenced song he had first called "Ida Red." In July 1954, at Sam Phillips' Sun Records, a young Elvis Presley recorded "That's All Right," a blues song by Arthur Crudup, drawing on country, gospel and blues at once. Britannica notes that Presley was careful to credit his Black sources.

title: The Electric Guitar
objective: After this level you can explain how an electric guitar's pickups and amplifier work.
summary: A pickup turns a steel string's vibration into a voltage at the same frequency, and an amplifier makes it loud. The 1931 Frying Pan came first; solid bodies tamed hollow-body feedback.

cards.headline: The guitar's first big problem wasn't talent. It was volume.
cards.body: As performance spaces grew, guitars became hard to hear over other instruments, especially horns. You can strum harder, but only so hard. The answer, starting in 1931, was to stop asking the wooden body to be loud and hand the job to electricity.

cards.headline: The Frying Pan
cards.body: In 1931, George Beauchamp and Adolph Rickenbacker built a guitar nicknamed the "Frying Pan," which became the first widely recognized electric guitar. Its secret was an electromagnetic pickup: a pair of horseshoe magnets arranged around the strings, with a coil of wire underneath. It looked like cookware. It sounded like the future.

mascot.line: Keep this chain: the string wiggles, the field changes, the voltage wiggles at the same pitch.

cards.headline: How a magnet hears a string
cards.body: Here's the physics. A steel string vibrating near the magnet changes the magnetic field running through the coil, and by Faraday's law that change pushes a small voltage through the wire. The voltage wiggles at the string's own frequency. Remember Level 3: pitch is frequency. So the note survives the trip into electricity, and an amplifier then makes the signal louder and sends it out through a speaker.

cards.headline: Why rock guitars went solid
cards.body: Early electric guitars had hollow bodies, and they suffered from distortion, overtones and feedback, so makers tried solid ones. Les Paul built a solid-body electric in the early 1940s, and by 1952 Fender and Gibson were both selling solid-body models. Distortion became a tool, too: an electric guitar's sound can be distorted on purpose. Remember "Rocket 88" from Level 73? Legend blames its fuzzy guitar on a damaged amplifier.

title: The Beatles
objective: After this level you can explain why the Beatles changed pop music.
summary: Liverpool's Beatles, steeped in American rock and roll, drew 73 million US viewers in 1964, held the Hot 100's top five, then left touring in 1966 to make the studio their instrument.

cards.headline: One night in 1964, 73 million Americans watched the same band.
cards.body: On February 9, 1964, the Beatles made their US television debut on The Ed Sullivan Show. That was more than 60 percent of everyone watching TV in the country that evening. How did four young musicians from Liverpool, England, get there, and what did they do with all that attention?

cards.headline: American music, sent back across the ocean
cards.body: The Beatles grew out of a shared love of American rock and roll. Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Fats Domino and Elvis Presley were among their inspirations, the same artists you met in Level 73, and Berry, Little Richard and Domino were Black pioneers of the style. So when Beatlemania reached America, part of what it carried was American music, played back with Liverpool accents.

cards.fact: On the Billboard Hot 100 dated April 4, 1964, the Beatles held all top five spots.
cards.context: At No. 1 that week was "Can't Buy Me Love." Behind the flood of hits sat a songwriting team inside the band: John Lennon and Paul McCartney wrote the Beatles' original songs together.

cards.headline: Then they stopped playing concerts
cards.body: In 1966, the Beatles quit performing live to concentrate on the recording studio. The result, Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band (1967), took months at EMI's Abbey Road studios, an unheard-of amount of time for a pop record, and its songs run into one another without the usual pause. Their producer, George Martin, called the studio a creative playground. It had become an instrument in its own right.

title: Motown and Soul
objective: After this level you can describe Motown and soul music.
summary: Berry Gordy founded Motown in Detroit in 1959 with an $800 loan and ran it like an assembly line. Soul returned to gospel and blues; Aretha Franklin's Respect (1967) became an anthem.

cards.headline: The Motor City built cars. Then a former assembly-line worker built hits.
cards.body: In January 1959, Berry Gordy Jr. founded a record company in Detroit with an $800 loan from his family. A two-story house on West Grand Boulevard became its studio and headquarters, nicknamed Hitsville. Motown grew into one of the most successful Black-owned businesses in American history. How do you build hits the way Detroit built cars?

cards.headline: A factory for songs
cards.body: Gordy said a brief stint on an auto-plant assembly line taught him how to make a quality product. So Motown ran like a line: in-house songwriting teams such as Holland-Dozier-Holland, a house band called the Funk Brothers, and strict quality control. Britannica credits Motown with the highest hit ratio for released singles of any record company in history. Its records were even mixed to sound good on car radios. Detroit, naturally.

cards.headline: Soul: back to church and the blues
cards.body: Alongside Motown's polish ran soul music, an African American style that grew from the 1950s into the 1970s. Britannica calls it a return to the roots of gospel and blues: church-style call and response, intense singing, long melodic runs. Ray Charles helped start it by turning gospel songs into secular ones. Remember Sister Rosetta Tharpe, who played gospel on electric guitar in Level 73? Same church, different road.

cards.headline: "Respect": one song, two movements
cards.body: Otis Redding wrote and first recorded "Respect." Aretha Franklin, raised singing in the Baptist church, reworked it: she spelled out R-E-S-P-E-C-T and added "sock it to me." It topped the Billboard Hot 100 on June 3, 1967, and became an anthem for civil rights and women's equality, even though Franklin said she had recorded it as a song about a man and a woman.

title: Festivals
objective: After this level you can describe music festivals from Woodstock onward.
summary: Woodstock (1969) drew about 400,000 to a farm in Bethel, New York, most without tickets, and ended with Hendrix's anthem. Live Aid (1985) linked London and Philadelphia for famine relief.

cards.headline: The Woodstock festival didn't happen in Woodstock.
cards.body: Woodstock ran August 15–18, 1969, on Max Yasgur's farm in Bethel, New York. The organizers kept the Woodstock name anyway. About 400,000 people showed up. What happens when that many people come to hear music in one field?

cards.headline: Mud, gate-crashers and a movie
cards.body: Not what anyone planned. Security was so thin that most people got in without paying, and rain turned the field to mud. The festival nearly bankrupted its four inexperienced promoters. What rescued them was a film: Michael Wadleigh's 1970 documentary was a commercial success that recouped their losses. The festival lost money; the movie of the festival made it back.

cards.headline: 9 a.m. Monday: Hendrix plays the anthem
cards.body: Jimi Hendrix didn't take the stage until around 9 a.m. on Monday, August 18, by which time many festivalgoers had already left. His "Star-Spangled Banner" used the electric guitar to act out the words: rockets and bombs bursting, a siren-like wail. Musicians call this text painting, music that paints what the lyrics say.

cards.headline: From one field to the whole planet
cards.body: Sixteen years later, a festival didn't even need a single field. Live Aid, on July 13, 1985, ran at the same time at Wembley Stadium in London and JFK Stadium in Philadelphia, raising money for famine relief in Ethiopia, and it was broadcast worldwide. The audience was no longer just the people standing in front of the stage.

title: Punk and Metal
objective: After this level you can describe punk and heavy metal.
summary: The power chord (root plus fifth, no third) drives heavy metal, codified in the 1970s by Zeppelin, Deep Purple and Sabbath, and punk (1975–80), which stripped rock down in New York and London.

cards.headline: Two of rock's loudest styles run on a chord with only two notes.
cards.body: Heavy metal and punk can sound like opposites: one heavy and virtuosic, the other short, fast and raw. Yet the power chord is a staple of both. Its trick is what it leaves out.

mascot.line: Leave out the third and you dodge the whole happy-or-sad question.

cards.headline: The power chord: a chord with a gap
cards.body: A power chord is just two notes: a root and the fifth above it. Remember Level 7? Major and minor chords differ in their middle note, the third. A power chord leaves the third out, so it's neither major nor minor. That's handy through heavy distortion, where full chords turn to mud but a power chord stays clear.

cards.headline: Heavy metal: rock, made heavier
cards.body: In the mid-1960s, British bands Cream and the Yardbirds and the guitarist Jimi Hendrix pushed rock toward a heavier sound. In the 1970s, Led Zeppelin, Deep Purple and Black Sabbath set the style: amplified distortion, heavy riffs and power chords, all on a blues-based foundation. The phrase "heavy metal" turned up in a 1968 Steppenwolf song before critics adopted it for the music.

cards.headline: Punk: rock, stripped to the bone
cards.body: Punk went the other way. It came together between 1975 and 1980, in New York and London at about the same time. At New York's CBGB club, the Ramones' 1976 debut album became the blueprint; in Britain, the Sex Pistols' 1977 hits made the country punk's epicenter. The songs were short, fast and minimal, a rejection of rock's polished production, and punk fueled a wave of independent record labels.

title: Music Videos
objective: After this level you can explain how music videos changed pop.
summary: MTV launched on August 1, 1981, and made image as important as sound. Michael Jackson's videos helped break racial barriers, and Thriller became the first music video in the National Film Registry.

cards.headline: MTV's very first video was called "Video Killed the Radio Star."
cards.body: MTV went on the air just after midnight on August 1, 1981, and the first clip it played was that song by the Buggles. Remember Level 72, when radio made national hits? Now a TV channel wanted the job. Did pictures really change what a hit was?

cards.headline: Now a song needed a look
cards.body: MTV played music videos continuously, introduced by video disc jockeys, or VJs. Britannica sums up the effect: visual presentation became as important as the music in selling records. A band's look, its moves and its little movie now helped decide whether you bought the song.

cards.headline: Michael Jackson changes the channel
cards.body: At first MTV struggled. Its fortunes changed when it added rhythm and blues artists, and Michael Jackson's videos for "Billie Jean" and "Beat It" showed that MTV exposure could make an artist a huge star. Britannica credits "Beat It" with helping break down the barriers between Black and white artists on radio and in music videos.

cards.fact: In 2009, Michael Jackson's "Thriller" became the first music video added to the National Film Registry.
cards.context: Directed by John Landis, the 1983 video runs about 14 minutes, more short horror film than song clip. The twist: by the mid-1990s, most of MTV's own schedule wasn't music at all, but reality shows, game shows and cartoons.

title: Checkpoint: Rock and Pop
objective: After this level you can trace popular music from the phonograph to the music video.
summary: The National Recording Registry adds 25 recordings a year, each at least 10 years old, and holds this chapter's story, from Scott's phonautograms to Rocket 88, Elvis at Sun, Respect and Sgt. Pepper.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 finale: the sounds America decided never to lose.
cards.body: The Library of Congress keeps a list of recordings worth saving for good. Walk through it and you'll bump into this whole chapter, from a sheet of soot-covered paper to a Beatles album. Here's how the list works, and what it says about the road from phonograph to music video.

cards.fact: Each year the Librarian of Congress adds 25 recordings to the National Recording Registry.
cards.context: The registry comes from the National Recording Preservation Act of 2000. A recording must be at least 10 years old and "culturally, historically or aesthetically significant." So this year's biggest new hit, however huge, will have to wait its turn.

Rock and roll merged rhythm and blues with country, led by Black pioneers. The electric guitar's pickup turned vibrating strings into a signal an amplifier could make loud. And MTV made how a song looked as important as how it sounded. Each new machine changed who could hear music, and how.

title: Hip-Hop Begins
objective: After this level you can explain how hip-hop began at Bronx block parties.
summary: Hip-hop is commonly dated to Kool Herc's August 11, 1973 Bronx party. Built by Black and Latino youth with Jamaican sound-system roots, it has four elements: DJing, MCing, breaking, graffiti.

cards.headline: Hip-hop's birthday party raised money for back-to-school clothes.
cards.body: On August 11, 1973, Cindy Campbell threw a back-to-school jam in the rec room of her apartment building at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue in the Bronx, to raise money for new school clothes. Her brother Clive, calling himself DJ Kool Herc, played the records. That night is the date most often given for the birth of hip-hop. So who was the DJ, and what did he start?

cards.headline: The DJ came from Kingston, Jamaica
cards.body: Herc was born in Kingston, Jamaica, and moved to the Bronx in 1967. Growing up, he'd soaked in Kingston's dance-hall parties and the powerful sound systems their deejays built, and he brought the idea north: his was the loudest sound system in the neighborhood. Jamaican deejays also "toasted," rapping improvised rhymes over the music. Hold on to that one. Talking over records is about to become an art of its own.

cards.headline: Built by the Bronx's Black and Latino youth
cards.body: The South Bronx of the early 1970s was hit hard by poverty. That's where hip-hop grew, made by the neighborhood's Black and Latino young people. The Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture traces it to African American, Afro-Caribbean and Afro-Latino traditions coming together in New York, and the Library of Congress describes the same thing: a new form of expression for Black and Latino youth. Nobody handed these kids a studio. They built a music out of parties.

mascot.line: Hip-hop isn't only rap. Keep all four in mind: DJing, MCing, breaking and graffiti.

cards.headline: Hip-hop is four arts, not one
cards.body: Hip-hop is a whole culture with four core parts: DJing, working the turntables; MCing, or rapping; breaking, the dance often called breakdancing; and graffiti. Herc even named the dancers. The ones who took the floor during a record's breaks, its percussive instrumental stretches, became break-boys and break-girls: b-boys and b-girls. So when someone says hip-hop, they might mean a song, a dance or a painted wall.

title: DJs and Sampling
objective: After this level you can explain how DJs and sampling build new music from old records.
summary: Herc's merry-go-round looped drum breaks on two turntables (the breakbeat); Theodore found scratching in 1975. Sampling reuses recordings; Funky Drummer is the most sampled break.

cards.headline: The best part of a funk record lasted only a few seconds.
cards.body: Kool Herc noticed that the breaks, the percussive instrumental stretches of funk records, brought the most people out to dance. Then the break would end and the song would move on. His fix turned the record player into an instrument.

cards.headline: The merry-go-round: two copies, one endless break
cards.body: Herc set up two turntables and a mixer and played two copies of the same record. As the break finished on one, he started it on the other, then back again, looping those few seconds so the dancers could keep going far longer. He called it the merry-go-round. Today that looped drum section has a name of its own: the breakbeat.

cards.headline: Scratching: a mistake worth keeping
cards.body: In 1975, a Bronx kid named Theodore Livingston was playing records in his bedroom when his mom came in to talk. Reaching to pause the record, he moved it back and forth under the needle, and he liked the rough sound it made. As Grand Wizzard Theodore, he's credited with inventing scratching, and one of his turntables is now in the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture.

cards.headline: Sampling: Herc's trick, done digitally
cards.body: Later, producers could grab sound electronically. Britannica defines digital sampling as music and sounds extracted from other recordings, and hip-hop's backing tracks often use it. The favorite ingredient is still a drum break. Clyde Stubblefield's 20-second drum solo on James Brown's 1970 single "Funky Drummer" has been called the most sampled drum break in music. The drummer's name may be new to you. His groove probably isn't.
