title: Rap
objective: After this level you can explain rhyme and flow in rap.
summary: Rap is rhythmic, rhyming speech over music; Rapper's Delight (1979) took it national. Flow is how words land on the beat: early rap rhymed on beat four, later rap roamed.

cards.headline: Rap turns the talking voice into an instrument.
cards.body: No strings, no keys, no singing required. Britannica defines rap as rhythmic, rhyming speech chanted to musical accompaniment. It sounds simple. The skill is in exactly where each word lands.

cards.headline: From Bronx parties to the national charts
cards.body: Remember Level 81's Jamaican toasting, deejays rapping improvised rhymes over the music? Rap grew up in African American communities in New York City. It reached the whole country with the Sugarhill Gang's "Rapper's Delight" in 1979, which climbed to No. 36 on the Billboard Hot 100. In 2011, the Library of Congress added it to its National Recording Registry.

mascot.line: This is Level 4's idea again: the beat stays put, and the words are the rhythm on top.

cards.headline: Flow: where the words land
cards.body: Music theorist Kyle Adams defines flow as all the rhythmic and articulation choices in a rapper's delivery: where syllables fall against the beat, which ones get stressed, how crisp or smooth they sound. Remember Level 4: the beat ticks steadily underneath, and rhythm is the pattern laid over it. In rap, the words are that rhythm. Same beat, different flow, completely different song.

cards.fact: Early-1980s rappers usually landed their rhymes on beat four.
cards.context: Analyses of early rap find rhymed line endings falling on or near the fourth beat, bar after bar, as regular as a clock chime. Later rappers broke the pattern: rhymes inside lines, rhymes off the beat, accents in surprising places. The rhymes got harder to predict, and more fun to chase.

title: Synthesizers
objective: After this level you can explain how a synthesizer makes sound.
summary: A synth's oscillator sets pitch, its filter removes harmonics to shape timbre, and its envelope (ADSR) shapes loudness. Moog unveiled his modular synth in 1964; the Minimoog came in 1970.

cards.headline: A synthesizer makes a note out of electricity alone.
cards.body: No string vibrates, no pipe fills with air. Inside, circuits manipulate electrical currents to generate a sound, which a speaker finally turns into air pressure. Three parts do the shaping, and each is a knob you can learn to hear.

cards.headline: The oscillator sets the pitch
cards.body: An oscillator makes a repeating electrical wave. Remember Level 3: pitch is frequency, how many times per second something vibrates. On Robert Moog's synthesizer, pressing a key sent the oscillator a voltage that depended on which key you pressed, and that set the pitch. Some wave shapes are rich: a sawtooth wave contains all the harmonics of its note, higher frequencies stacked on top. That gives the next step something to carve.

mascot.line: Don't mix these two up: the oscillator sets the pitch, the filter changes the color.

cards.headline: The filter carves the tone
cards.body: Next comes the filter, which removes some of those harmonics. It changes the note's color, what musicians call timbre, while the oscillator keeps the pitch. Starting from a rich wave and filtering part of it away is called subtractive synthesis. Think of a sculptor with a block of marble: the sound is in there, and the filter chips away the rest.

cards.headline: The envelope shapes the note in time
cards.body: Last, an envelope controls how loud the note is from moment to moment, in four stages. Attack: the rise when you press the key. Decay: the fall to a steady level. Sustain: that level, held while your finger stays down. Release: the fade after you let go. Stretch out the attack and the note swells in gently instead of starting at full volume.

title: Electronic Dance Music
objective: After this level you can describe disco, house and techno.
summary: Disco grew in early-1970s New York clubs on a four-on-the-floor kick; house grew from it in Chicago, named after the Warehouse; Detroit techno (1985) was instrumental and complex.

cards.headline: In 1979, Chicago tried to bury disco. Then Chicago brought it back.
cards.body: Disco Demolition Night, held in Chicago in 1979, became the symbol of a fierce backlash against disco. Yet within a few years, Chicago DJs were building a new dance music out of disco's parts. Follow the kick drum and you'll find three cities on one family tree.

cards.headline: New York: disco and the DJ
cards.body: Disco grew in underground New York City clubs in the early 1970s, rooms that welcomed mostly Black, Latino and gay dancers. DJs used extended 12-inch singles to build long mixes that kept people moving. Under it all ran the four-on-the-floor: a bass drum on every one of the four beats in a bar. Remember Level 4's beat, the steady pulse? Here you feel it in your chest.

cards.headline: Chicago: house, named after a club
cards.body: From 1977, DJ Frankie Knuckles played the Warehouse, a members-only Chicago club for Black gay dancers. He re-edited disco records on reel-to-reel tape to stretch out their grooves, and the music became known as house, after the club. In the early 1980s house blended disco's soul vocals and four-to-the-floor kick with synthesizer sounds. By 1986 it had reached Europe.

cards.headline: Detroit: techno
cards.body: In Detroit, three young African American DJ-producers, Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson, began drawing attention in 1985. Inspired partly by the German electro-pop band Kraftwerk, their techno had glacial synth melodies and brisk machine rhythms. Unlike house, it was mostly instrumental, and its beats were more complex than house's steady kick. Same family, cooler temperature.

title: Reggae
objective: After this level you can describe reggae and Bob Marley.
summary: Reggae came from western Kingston in the late 1960s, after ska and rocksteady, with choppy offbeat chords. Bob Marley carried it worldwide; UNESCO listed it as heritage in 2018.

cards.headline: UNESCO lists reggae as part of humanity's cultural heritage.
cards.body: In 2018, UNESCO added the reggae music of Jamaica to its list of the world's intangible cultural heritage. The style itself was young: it was born in Jamaica in the late 1960s, in marginalized communities of western Kingston. How did it travel so far, so fast?

cards.headline: Ska, rocksteady, reggae: and the offbeat
cards.body: Reggae grew out of earlier Jamaican styles: ska became rocksteady, which became reggae. Its signature is the offbeat. Drums and bass drive a heavy four-beat rhythm, while the rhythm guitar or keyboard plays short, choppy chords on the offbeats instead of the main beats. Listen for that chunk off the beat. It's reggae's fingerprint.

cards.headline: Bob Marley carries it worldwide
cards.body: Bob Marley, born in 1945 in Nine Miles, Jamaica, formed the Wailers in Trench Town with Peter Tosh and Bunny Wailer, writing songs for and about poor West Indians. Reggae's lyrics took on social and economic injustice, and through the Wailers it became linked with the Rastafari movement. After they signed with Island Records in 1972, their album Catch a Fire carried reggae worldwide. Marley died in 1981, at just 36.

cards.fact: In 1978, Bob Marley got two political rivals to join hands onstage.
cards.context: Jamaica was torn by political violence. At the One Love Peace Concert in Kingston, Marley brought Prime Minister Michael Manley and opposition leader Edward Seaga onstage and held their joined hands up high. For one night, a reggae concert was a peace summit.

cards.headline: Echoes in the Bronx
cards.body: Remember Kool Herc, the Kingston-born DJ with the loudest sound system in his Bronx neighborhood? Britannica counts hip-hop among the styles reggae influenced, along with dancehall. Herc carried Jamaica's sound-system parties and toasting north, and Bronx kids turned them into something new.

title: Global Pop
objective: After this level you can explain how pop music from Korea, Nigeria and Latin America went global.
summary: Pop crossed borders without English: BTS topped the Billboard 200 in 2018, Afrobeats (not Fela's Afrobeat) reached the Hot 100, and Despacito led the Hot 100 for 16 weeks.

cards.headline: In 2018, America's No. 1 album was sung mostly in Korean.
cards.body: BTS's Love Yourself: Tear topped the Billboard 200 album chart, the first time a K-pop act had done it. It's one of three stories in this level, from South Korea, Nigeria and Latin America, about pop crossing the world without switching to English.

cards.headline: K-pop: English came last
cards.body: BTS was assembled by producer Bang Si-Hyuk's Big Hit Entertainment, starting in 2010. They sang about self-love, individuality and empowerment, mostly in Korean, and topped the album chart that way. Their first English-language song, "Dynamite," only arrived in 2020, when it debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. The fame came first; the English came later.

cards.headline: Afrobeats: mind the "s"
cards.body: Afrobeats grew up in Nigeria and Ghana in the early 2000s, mixing highlife, dancehall and soca into upbeat dance pop about love, success and partying. Mind the "s": Afrobeat, without it, is Fela Kuti's 1960s and 70s blend of Yoruba music with jazz and funk, known for its political bite. In 2016 Drake's "One Dance," featuring Wizkid, topped the Hot 100 for 10 weeks, and in 2021 Nigeria's Burna Boy won the Grammy for Best Global Music Album.

cards.headline: Latin pop: the "Despacito" summer
cards.body: In 2017, Luis Fonsi and Daddy Yankee's Spanish-language "Despacito" (with a remix featuring Justin Bieber) led the Billboard Hot 100 for 16 weeks. That tied the record at the time, and no mostly non-English song had ever held the top spot longer. America's biggest singles chart no longer needed English to crown a winner.

title: Studio Tricks
objective: After this level you can explain what studio effects like Auto-Tune do.
summary: Auto-Tune moves a sung note to the nearest semitone: a quiet fix, or a robot voice when pushed, as on Cher's Believe (1998). Studios add reverb; a drier voice seems closer.

cards.headline: Cher's robot voice came from a tool built to hide mistakes.
cards.body: On her 1998 hit "Believe," Cher's voice leaps from note to note like a machine. It was the first commercial recording to show off Auto-Tune's side effects on purpose. The tool was designed to fix singing quietly, and its inventor came from the oil business.

cards.headline: From oil fields to vocal booths
cards.body: Andy Hildebrand spent 1976 to 1989 interpreting seismic data for the oil industry. Later, his company Antares released Auto-Tune. It detects the pitch of each sung note and moves it to the nearest semitone: the smallest step on a keyboard, from one key to the very next, as you saw in Level 7. A slightly flat note gets nudged back into tune.

cards.headline: Invisible fix or robot effect
cards.body: Used gently, pitch correction tidies a vocal and you never notice. Push it hard and the voice leaps from note to note while staying perfectly, unnaturally in tune: the "Believe" sound. Engineers realized the side effect could be a style. Today both uses, the quiet fix and the obvious robot, are common in recorded music.

cards.headline: Reverb: a room in a box
cards.body: Reverberation is sound that lingers after its source stops, built from reflections bouncing around a space. Studios often record in dry rooms lined with absorbent material, then add reverb afterward with metal plates, springs or digital algorithms. The balance sets the scene: the stronger the dry sound, the closer the singer seems. A voice recorded in a tiny booth can end up sounding like it's in a grand hall.

title: From Records to Streaming
objective: After this level you can explain how music moved from records to MP3s to streaming.
summary: The CD (1982) samples 44,100 times a second to cover hearing up to 20 kHz; MP3 drops what you can't hear; streaming made up 82% of US recorded-music revenue in 2025.

cards.headline: In 2025, 82% of US recorded-music money came from streaming.
cards.body: That's the Recording Industry Association of America's count, measured at wholesale. Getting from discs on a shelf to songs that arrive through a phone took three big ideas.

cards.headline: Idea 1: turn sound into numbers
cards.body: Sony and Philips brought the compact disc to market in 1982. A CD stores sound as digital data, microscopic pits and flat spots read by a laser. It measures the sound wave 44,100 times every second. Why so many? To capture a frequency, you must sample more than twice as often, and remember Level 3: hearing tops out around 20 kHz. Twice that is 40,000, and the CD adds a little headroom.

cards.headline: Idea 2: throw away what you can't hear
cards.body: Researchers at Germany's Fraunhofer institute found a shortcut: store the parts of a sound your ear can't perceive with less precision. Their MP3 files came out up to ten times smaller, with virtually no audible difference. The team chose the name ".mp3" by email poll on July 14, 1995. In 1999, college student Shawn Fanning's Napster let people share music files over the internet, until a court fight with the record industry shut it down in 2001.

cards.headline: Idea 3: stream it, don't store it
cards.body: Spotify, founded in Sweden, launched in 2008 and streamed songs instead of selling files: free with ads, or paid without them. That model won. The RIAA put streaming at 82% of US recorded-music revenue in 2025. Discs, then files, then streams: each step made music lighter to carry, until it weighed nothing at all.

title: Checkpoint: Hip-Hop, Electronic and Beyond

summary: Roland's TR-808 (1980) synthesized drums from circuits; dismissed and discontinued, it powered Planet Rock (1982). Turntables, synths and computers remade music, often by accident.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 finale: the drum machine the critics dismissed.
cards.body: Roland's TR-808 came out in 1980. Critics complained it didn't sound like real drums, and Roland stopped making it after selling about 12,000. Then hip-hop producers got hold of it. Its story ties together this whole chapter's machines.

cards.headline: Drums built from circuits
cards.body: The 808 didn't play recordings of drums. Roland's engineers used analog synthesis, manipulating electrical currents like Level 84's synthesizers, to make sounds that imitated hand-claps and bass notes. That's why critics called it fake, and why its thundering bass became famous. In 1982, Afrika Bambaataa and the Soul Sonic Force's "Planet Rock," made with an 808, became one of the decade's most influential records.

title: Music and the Brain
objective: After this level you can explain what happens in the brain when we hear music.
summary: Hair cells send signals up the auditory nerve to the temporal lobes. A steady beat stirs movement areas, chills release dopamine, and the Mozart effect was brief.

cards.headline: Your favorite song and a good meal share a brain chemical.
cards.body: When a piece of music gives you chills, your brain releases dopamine, a chemical also involved in the pleasure of rewards like food. Scientists caught it happening in 2011. But before a song can thrill you, it has to get into your head at all. Let's follow it in.

cards.headline: Your ears collect the sound; your brain hears it
cards.body: Remember Level 10's cochlea, where hair cells sort pitch like keys along a piano? Those hair cells turn the vibration into an electrical signal. The auditory nerve carries that signal to the brain, and the brain turns it into a sound you recognize. Its receiving desk is an area at the top of each temporal lobe. Until the signal arrives there, a song is just a pattern of electricity.

cards.headline: Sitting still, part of you is dancing
cards.body: Hearing is only the start. In a 2007 brain-imaging study, listeners heard different rhythms while lying still. Rhythms with a regular beat, the steady pulse from Level 4, drove extra activity in movement areas of the brain: the basal ganglia and the supplementary motor area. Nobody was moving. So when you say a song makes you want to move, your brain agrees. It has already started.

cards.headline: The chills are chemistry
cards.body: Back to the hook. In that 2011 study, music that gave listeners chills released dopamine in the striatum, deep in the brain. The timing was the surprise. At the peak moment, the release centered on one region, the nucleus accumbens. In the run-up, while listeners anticipated the peak, it came from another, the caudate. Your brain pays out twice: once for the big moment, and once for the wait.

mascot.line: This is Level 38's myth again. Enjoy Mozart; just don't expect him to make you smarter.

cards.fact: Playing Mozart won't make you smarter.
cards.context: In 1993, students did better on a spatial-reasoning task right after hearing a Mozart sonata, but the boost faded within about 15 minutes. A 2010 analysis of nearly 40 studies found little evidence of any special Mozart effect, and other music did about as well. Music does remarkable things in the brain; this just isn't one of them.

title: Why Songs Get Stuck
objective: After this level you can explain why some songs get stuck in your head.
summary: About 9 in 10 people get a weekly earworm, usually a looping snippet. Sticky tunes are faster, with a familiar shape and one odd leap. Listening, distraction or gum can help.

cards.headline: About 9 in 10 people get a song stuck in their head every week.
cards.body: That's from a survey of more than 12,000 people in Finland. Scientists call it involuntary musical imagery; everyone else calls it an earworm. So why does one tune move in and refuse to leave, while another never visits at all?

cards.headline: It's a loop, not a song
cards.body: Notice what actually plays in your head. It's rarely the whole track, start to finish. Most earworms are short snippets of a larger tune, a line or two that ends and starts again. That's part of why they're so hard to shake: a snippet has no ending to wrap things up, so round it goes, like a GIF of a song.

cards.headline: The recipe for a sticky tune
cards.body: In 2016, researchers asked 3,000 people which songs got stuck in their heads, then compared those songs with similarly popular ones nobody named. The earworms tended to be faster. Their melodies had a common overall shape, Level 5's contour, the kind your ear already knows. And they had something unusual too: a surprising leap or repetition. Familiar shape, one odd twist: that's the hook that catches.

cards.fact: The song people named most often: Lady Gaga's "Bad Romance."
cards.context: Next came Journey's "Don't Stop Believin'" and Kylie Minogue's "Can't Get You Out of My Head", a title that doubles as a confession. Sorry if one of them just moved in.

cards.headline: How to evict one
cards.body: In a 2014 study, the most popular and effective responses were surprisingly simple: listen to the tune itself, or distract yourself with other music or with words. Another option came from a 2015 University of Reading study: chew gum. It cut down on stuck songs, likely because chewing keeps busy the mouth-movement planning you use to sing a tune silently in your head.

title: Music and Emotion
objective: After this level you can explain why music can make us feel happy or sad.
summary: Music borrows the voice's code: sad is slow, soft and low. Culture tunes cues like major and minor. Sad songs please when safe, and a few people get little joy from music.

cards.headline: A piece with no words can still sound heartbroken.
cards.body: Nobody in a cello solo sings "I'm sad." There are no words at all. So how can a few notes sound like grief? Part of the answer is older than any song. It's in the way people talk.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing: music borrows the voice's code. Slow, soft and low sounds sad.

cards.headline: Music speaks in the voice's code
cards.body: A 2003 review pooled 104 studies of emotional voices and 41 of music performance, and found the two use similar cues. Sadness comes out slow, soft and low, in speech and in music alike. Happiness comes out fast, loud and high. So when a cello sounds heartbroken, it's doing what a sad voice does. You already speak this language; music just sings it.

cards.headline: Culture tunes some of the code
cards.body: Not every cue works that way. Remember Level 7: young children first judged happy and sad music by tempo alone, and only later by major and minor. And in Papua New Guinea, hearing major as happier was strongly tied to how much Western-style music people knew. Speed seems to speak early and widely; the mood of a minor key is partly learned.

cards.headline: Why a sad song can feel good
cards.body: Here's the puzzle: why would anyone choose to feel sad? A 2015 review found sadness from music is enjoyed when it feels non-threatening, when the music is beautiful, and when it helps, for example by easing a mood. The key is that in art, the real loss isn't there. A sad song lets you feel the storm from indoors.

cards.fact: Some people with normal hearing get little pleasure from music.
cards.context: A 2014 study described healthy people who heard music normally but got little pleasure from it, and their bodies showed no response to music others loved. Yet winning money pleased them just fine. Remember Level 91's musical chills? For them, music simply doesn't deliver that reward.

title: Film Music
objective: After this level you can explain how film scores shape what we feel.
summary: Silent films had live music. Jaws's two neighboring notes, E and F, stand in for a shark we rarely see. In a 2001 study, music changed how viewers read the same scene.

cards.headline: Silent films were never silent.
cards.body: Through the silent era, a pianist, a theater organist or, in big cities, a whole orchestra played live beside the screen. Before movies could talk, they already had music. So what is music doing to you while you watch?

cards.headline: Two notes, one shark
cards.body: For Jaws (1975), John Williams built the shark's theme from just two notes, E and F, alternating over and over. Remember Level 6? Two neighboring keys like E and F make a second, the kind of interval traditional theory counts as dissonant: tension with no release. As the shark closes in, the two notes grow louder and faster. You feel it coming before you see a thing.

cards.fact: In Jaws, the shark doesn't appear until the film's 81st minute.
cards.context: The mechanical sharks kept breaking down, so for most of the film the shark is suggested rather than shown. Williams's two notes do the work: hear them, and you know it's there. The score won him an Academy Award.

cards.headline: Same scene, different story
cards.body: In a 2001 study, people watched ambiguous film clips with upbeat music, gloomy music or none. With upbeat music, they read the scenes more positively; with gloomy music, more negatively; with no music, fairly neutrally. A week later, their memories of the clips leaned the same way as the music. A score doesn't just decorate a scene. It tells you what the scene means.

title: Video Game Music
objective: After this level you can describe how game music grew from beeps to orchestras.
summary: Koji Kondo wrote Super Mario Bros. for three notes at once, with music that reacts to play. It became the first game music in the National Recording Registry in 2023.

cards.headline: In 2023, a video game tune joined America's archive of sound treasures.
cards.body: The Library of Congress added Koji Kondo's Super Mario Bros. theme, from 1985, to its National Recording Registry: the first video game music ever chosen. Not bad for music written for a very limited machine. Here's how game music got from beeps to that honor.

cards.headline: Three notes and a hiss
cards.body: Kondo later described what he had to work with: just three musical notes at a time, plus one white-noise sound, and very little data for music at all. Remember Level 1's harmony, notes sounding together? A single three-note chord would have used every voice the machine had. So every note had to earn its place, and Kondo made it sound effortless.

cards.headline: Music that plays along with you
cards.body: Film music follows a fixed story; game music has to follow you. Kondo wrote jingles to cheer players on after a Game Over, fanfares for reaching a goal, and pieces that sped up when time was running short. That last one is Level 4's tempo put to work: the clock is ticking, and the music makes sure you feel it.

cards.headline: From sound chip to concert hall
cards.body: Those three-voice tunes didn't stay in the console. Kondo's Super Mario Bros. music has been performed by orchestras around the globe. And in 2023 the Grammys handed out their first award for video game scores, won by Stephanie Economou for Assassin's Creed Valhalla: Dawn of Ragnarok. Game music had graduated.

title: Who Gets Paid
objective: After this level you can explain how songwriters get paid and what copyright protects.
summary: A recorded song holds two copyrights: the musical work and the sound recording. US AM/FM radio pays only the songwriters' side. Each 2026 CD or download copy earns 13.1 cents.

cards.headline: Someone was charging for "Happy Birthday."
cards.body: For years, Warner/Chappell Music collected licensing fees for "Happy Birthday to You." Then filmmakers sued, and in 2015 a federal judge ruled the company held no valid copyright to the lyrics. So who really owns a song, and who gets paid when you hear it?

cards.headline: Every recorded song holds two copyrights

mascot.line: People mix these two up all the time: the song is one copyright, the recording another.

cards.headline: The song and the recording are different things
cards.body: US copyright splits every recorded song in two. The musical work is the song on paper: melody, harmony and lyrics, the stuff of Level 1, written by songwriters. The sound recording is one particular performance of it, captured by performers and producers. They're commonly owned and licensed separately. Cover a song and you make a new recording, but the song still belongs to its writers.

cards.headline: The radio gap
cards.body: A musical work's copyright includes public performance, like radio play, which songwriters usually license through organizations such as ASCAP and BMI. But in the US, the performance right for sound recordings covers only digital transmissions, like streaming and satellite radio. So when a hit plays on AM/FM radio, the songwriters' side gets paid, and the recording's side gets nothing.

cards.fact: In 2026, each CD, vinyl or download copy of a US song earns its owners 13.1 cents.
cards.context: That's the statutory "mechanical" royalty set by the Copyright Royalty Judges for copying the musical work. Songs longer than five minutes can earn more, at 2.52 cents per minute.

title: Learning an Instrument
objective: After this level you can explain what practice does for a musician.
summary: The best Berlin student violinists reported the most solo practice. Deliberate practice is focused and feedback-driven, but practice explains only part of skill, about 21% in music.

cards.headline: Why are the best violinists better than the rest?
cards.body: In 1993, psychologists put that question to a Berlin music academy. They grouped violin students as the best, the good, or future music teachers, and asked each one to estimate how much they had practiced over the years. The answer made practice famous. Then it got more complicated.

cards.headline: The best had practiced the most
cards.body: The difference showed up in the hours spent practicing alone. By age 18, the best students reported about 7,400 hours; the future music teachers, about 3,400. That's more than twice as much. The researchers, led by Anders Ericsson, concluded that practice was a big part of what separated them.

mascot.line: Don't chase a number of hours. Find the bar you keep fumbling, and slow it down.

cards.headline: Not all practice is equal
cards.body: Ericsson called the key ingredient deliberate practice: effortful work designed to improve, with well-defined tasks, set at the right difficulty, and informative feedback. That's different from play. Running your favorite piece top to bottom for fun is playing. Slowing down the one bar you keep fumbling, fixing it and checking it again: that's deliberate practice.

cards.headline: Practice matters. It isn't everything.
cards.body: Later research added a twist. A 2014 meta-analysis found deliberate practice explained about 21% of the differences in music performance. And a 2019 repeat of the Berlin study found no significant practice gap between the best and the good violinists. Practice clearly helps, and it's the part you control. It just isn't the whole story.

title: Perfect Pitch
objective: After this level you can explain perfect pitch and how rare it is.
summary: Absolute pitch, naming a note with no reference, is under 1 in 10,000 in the US and Europe, and far more common among Mandarin speakers who trained early. Most people use relative pitch.

cards.headline: Play a random note, and a few people can simply name it.
cards.body: No piano to check against, no starting note: they hear it and say "that's an A." It's called absolute pitch, or perfect pitch: naming or singing a note without any reference note. How rare is it, and why do some people have it?

cards.headline: Rarer than you'd think
cards.body: In the US and Europe, absolute pitch is estimated at fewer than 1 in 10,000 people. And it isn't a musical superpower. Having it doesn't necessarily make someone better at other musical tasks. A person with perfect pitch might hear Level 3's 440 Hz tone and instantly call it A, and still struggle with rhythm. It's a rare ear, not a guarantee.

mascot.line: Don't mix these up: perfect pitch names a lone note; relative pitch hears the distances.

cards.headline: What the rest of us use
cards.body: Remember Level 5? You recognize "Twinkle, Twinkle" starting on any note, because you hear the relationships between notes. That's relative pitch, and nearly everyone uses it. Even without perfect pitch, most people have a surprisingly accurate long-term memory for pitch, as long as they don't need to name the note. You may not know it's an A. You still remember how it sounds.

cards.headline: The language clue
cards.body: A 2006 study tested music students at the Central Conservatory in Beijing, who spoke Mandarin, and at the Eastman School in New York. In both, absolute pitch was more common the earlier training began. But at every starting age, it was far more common among the Mandarin speakers. In Mandarin, pitch changes meaning: "ma" can mean mother, hemp, horse or a scolding, depending on its tone.

title: How to Really Listen
objective: After this level you can use a simple method to listen closely to any piece of music.
summary: Copland's three planes: sensuous, expressive, sheerly musical. Listen in passes (beat, melody, harmony), and closely rather than loudly: WHO allows 80 dB for 40 hours a week.

cards.headline: Are you just listening, or listening for something?
cards.body: In 1939, the American composer Aaron Copland wrote a book called What to Listen for in Music. His goal was to turn passive listeners into active ones: not someone who is just listening, "but someone who is listening for something." Here is his map, a method built from this tree, and one rule to protect your ears.

items.label: Sensuous
points: The pleasure of the sound itself

items.label: Expressive
points: What the music makes you feel

cards.headline: Listen in three passes
cards.body: Copland noticed that casual listeners catch the melody first, then the rhythm, and take harmony and tone color for granted. So give them turns. Pick one song. First pass: tap the beat (Level 4). Second: hum the melody (Level 5). Third: ignore the tune and follow the chords underneath (Level 6). Copland said we really hear on all three planes at once; the passes just train you to notice.

cards.headline: Listen closely, not loudly
cards.body: WHO says 80 decibels is safe for up to 40 hours a week, but at 90 decibels safe time drops to four hours: ten decibels louder cuts your time to a tenth. It suggests keeping your device at no more than 60% of maximum. Remember Level 10's hair cells, sorting pitch in the cochlea? Human hair cells don't grow back. But noise-induced hearing loss is completely preventable.

questions.explanation: Human hair cells don't grow back, so noise-induced hearing loss is permanent, though completely preventable.

title: Mastery Challenge: Music
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Music Levels 1–99 across the whole tree.
summary: Questions from How Music Works and Music and You: sound, rhythm, harmony and notation, then the brain, earworms, film and game music, royalties and pitch. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The Music Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Ten questions from across the tree, from air pressure and staff lines to chills, earworms and royalties. Level 1 asked what turns sound into music; now show how far you've followed it. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Music: mastered
learned: What happens in your brain when music gives you chills or makes you want to move.
Why music can sound happy or sad without words, and why a sad song can still feel good.
How film and game scores steer what you feel about what you see and play.
Who gets paid when a song plays, and what kind of practice actually makes you better.

questions.prompt: The 2019 Harvard-led study that found music in all 315 societies also found two song types everywhere. Which?

options.label: Lullabies and dance songs
Anthems and hymns
options.rationale: The study named lullabies and dance songs.

options.label: Work songs and marches
options.rationale: Not the pair the study named.

options.label: Love songs and laments
options.rationale: Not the pair the study named.

questions.explanation: Lullabies and dance songs turned up across the world's societies.

questions.prompt: You count 6 seconds between a lightning flash and its thunder. Roughly how far away was the strike?

options.label: About 200 meters
options.rationale: Sound travels much further in 6 seconds.

options.label: About 2 kilometers
About 6 kilometers
options.rationale: That would take about 18 seconds.

options.label: About 20 kilometers
options.rationale: Far too far for 6 seconds.

questions.explanation: Every 3 seconds is about a kilometer, so 6 seconds means about 2 km.

questions.prompt: What did the 2016 study of the Tsimane' in Bolivia find about consonant and dissonant chords?

options.label: They couldn't tell the two kinds apart
options.rationale: They could tell them apart.

options.label: They strongly preferred consonance
options.rationale: That was the American listeners.

options.label: They told them apart but liked both equally
They strongly preferred dissonance
options.rationale: They rated both equally pleasant.

questions.explanation: The Tsimane' distinguished the chords but rated them equally pleasant, so the preference seems learned.

questions.prompt: A drummer counts off a song at 120 BPM. How many beats go by each second?

options.label: One
options.rationale: That's 60 BPM.

options.label: Two
Four
options.rationale: That would be 240 BPM.

options.label: Twelve
options.rationale: Far too fast for 120 BPM.

questions.explanation: At 60 BPM one beat falls every second, and 120 BPM is twice as fast: two beats a second.

questions.prompt: On a treble staff, which letters do the four spaces spell, from bottom to top?

options.label: E, G, B, D
options.rationale: Those are the lines, not the spaces.

options.label: F, A, C, E
G, B, D, F
options.rationale: That skips the treble clef's pattern.

options.label: A, C, E, G
options.rationale: Not the treble clef's spaces.

questions.explanation: With the treble clef, the spaces spell F, A, C, E, and the lines read E, G, B, D, F.

questions.prompt: A friend plays Mozart before an exam to raise their intelligence. What does the research on the Mozart effect suggest?

options.label: It raises IQ for several weeks
options.rationale: The 1993 boost faded within about 15 minutes.

options.label: It works only for musicians
options.rationale: That isn't what the studies found.

options.label: Only Mozart's music works
options.rationale: Other music did about as well.

options.label: Little evidence of any special Mozart effect

questions.explanation: The original boost was brief and spatial, and a 2010 analysis of nearly 40 studies found little evidence of a special Mozart effect.

questions.prompt: Which everyday trick cut down on earworms in a 2015 University of Reading study?

options.label: Chewing gum
Humming a different note
options.rationale: The study tested chewing gum.

options.label: Covering one ear
options.rationale: Not what the study tested.

options.label: Drinking cold water
options.rationale: Not what the study tested.

questions.explanation: Chewing gum reduced stuck songs, likely by busying the mouth-movement planning used to sing silently.

questions.prompt: What is John Williams's famous shark theme for Jaws built from?

options.label: A full orchestra playing a major chord
options.rationale: It's far simpler than that.

options.label: Two alternating notes, E and F
A single note held without stopping
options.rationale: Two notes alternate.

options.label: A melody borrowed from a lullaby
options.rationale: Williams built it from two notes.

questions.explanation: The theme alternates E and F, growing louder and faster as the shark nears.

questions.prompt: Koji Kondo's NES music for Super Mario Bros. could sound how many musical notes at once, plus a noise sound?

options.label: One
options.rationale: He had more than one voice.

options.label: Three
Eight
options.rationale: He had fewer than that.

options.label: Sixteen
options.rationale: Far more than the machine offered.

questions.explanation: Kondo had three musical notes at a time plus one white-noise sound, and very little data.

questions.prompt: In 2026, what US statutory royalty does each CD or download copy of a five-minute-or-shorter song earn?

options.label: 0.1 cents
options.rationale: Far below the statutory rate.

options.label: 1.31 cents
options.rationale: Off by a factor of ten.

options.label: 13.1 cents

options.rationale: Far above the statutory rate.

questions.explanation: The 2026 US mechanical rate for physical copies and downloads is 13.1 cents per song, or 2.52 cents a minute if larger.
